This study investigates the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks for calculating the $m$-th eigenvalue of the three-dimensional Helmholtz operator under Dirichlet boundary conditions in a $120^3$ cube. We analyze how the average eigenvalue error evolves with new training sets, and compare this to the convergence of a Monte Carlo estimate in statistical mechanics, finding similar behavior in both cases. To understand this performance, we examine the effects of pre-training the network using Rayleigh-Feynman expansions and the impact of regularization on its output. These findings ultimately inform a theoretical assessment of generalization and suggest strategies for improving it. The study of cosmic ray arrival directions in the extremely energetic range has the potential to offer crucial insights into the origins and properties of these powerful particles. By analyzing a large dataset of 5011 cosmic events recorded over five years at the Pierre Auger Observatory, researchers discovered substantial anisotropies in cosmic ray distribution. Specifically, they found that the arrival directions of these cosmic events cluster around the centers of two distinct regions: "Ursa Major" at right ascension 251 degrees and "Pegasus" at 48 degrees. These regions correspond to regions in the Galactic Center sky map that exhibit enhanced densities of molecular gas. This study's findings indicate that the sources of extremely energetic cosmic events are likely grouped into two categories and that their combined flux accounts for a significant portion of anisotropic patterns observed in the cosmic ray spectrum. Furthermore, the researchers calculated that the probability of observing such anisotropic patterns, assuming random and uniform cosmic ray distribution, is less than 0.31% (3.7σ) if each region contributes equally, or less than 0.99% (1.5σ) if "Pegasus" dominates, if considering only right ascension variations. Additionally, further analysis of southern hemisphere data, encompassing 368 events, revealed anisotropic patterns centered at "Pavo" at right ascension 312 degrees, exhibiting similar characteristics to "Pegasus", thereby enhancing the overall significance to more than 2.7σ. These groundbreaking findings provide conclusive evidence of cosmic ray anisotropies above 4 EeV and open doors for further research in this energetic range, including the potential to discern contributions from two distinct types of ultra-high energy cosmic rays with different mass compositions. Moreover, these results may offer fresh insights into the physical mechanisms governing the high-energy particle production processes. This research introduces an approach to creating controllers for quadruped robots to navigate diverse environments using reinforcement learning. The underlying challenge in RL applications to navigation is generating feasible gait patterns to start the training process. Existing solutions involve developing specialized generators or adapting existing ones to specific environments, which may not be practical when dealing with complex environments like manipulation tasks. Our proposed method utilizes an evolutionary algorithm-based generator that can produce effective gait patterns suitable for a wide range of quadruped robots, even in new environments. When applied to the Boston Dynamics Spot robot, our controller obtained successful results for navigation in various environments, as evidenced by our experimental video. The evolution-based generator can generate controllers that are more stable than other generators based on RL, which is particularly beneficial in reinforcement learning where initial gait patterns play a crucial role in obtaining rewards. As a result, our approach offers a simpler and more efficient solution for RL applications to navigation and could be applied to other scenarios. Additionally, our controller obtained successful results for more complex tasks like traversing obstacles and climbing stairs. Road surfaces with cracks attract users' attention, which has been proven to be distracting and leads to potential safety issues. The current methods for automatic road surface condition assessment are limited to specific types of cracks and only focus on certain areas, whereas they fail to consider more complex scenarios such as unusual patterns, multiple cracks, and varied sizes. To address this issue, our research introduces a novel approach that can effectively identify cracks of all types and sizes across different regions. We employ a dynamic partitioning method to accurately divide the road into distinct areas and analyze them separately. As a result, our framework is capable of detecting cracks of varying lengths, densities, and patterns. To enhance performance, we utilize a weighted fusion strategy that combines features from different partitioned areas to improve overall results. Furthermore, we introduce a dynamic sampling method to optimize network training and prevent overfitting. Our framework has been successfully applied to the 300K image dataset, yielding a mean average precision of 0.9467, which significantly outperforms the existing methods. The source code for our framework is available at https://github.com/zhaozhanyu2018/READ.EXT.

Recent research has yielded contradictory evidence regarding the correlation between galaxy mass and halo mass, with many studies concluding that more massive galaxies reside within larger haloes, as predicted by theoretical models. Nevertheless, existing studies have primarily focused on galaxies at a single stage and have overlooked their evolution. To address this, we utilized data from the CANDELS project and performed a multi-wavelength analysis of over 8000 galaxies spanning a broad mass range at two distinct epochs, allowing us to investigate how galaxy mass correlates with halo mass at different stages. By comparing observed galaxy masses to theoretical predictions from the widely-used HYPERION model, we found a more substantial discrepancy at earlier times and more massive galaxy masses, indicating that this model underestimates the required halo mass for its production. Furthermore, we found that more massive galaxies at both stages require larger haloes to facilitate their formation, with lower-mass galaxies requiring fewer haloes and less energy to produce the same amount of stellar mass. When considering the impact of bulge formation on galaxy mass and halo correlations, we found that it introduces additional scatter, although it does not alter the overall trend. To reconcile these findings with previous research, we suggest that the observed halo mass discrepancy may be attributed to the effects of feedback, particularly at earlier times and for more massive galaxies, where it may give rise to extended halo masses that expand as gas is removed. Consequently, the extended halo mass of massive galaxies could lead to the observed correlation between galaxy mass and halo mass at later stages, although this requires further investigation. To further explore these findings, we recommend examining the relationship between galaxy mass and halo mass at earlier stages using data from the AKARI-2DHH2D survey. If confirmed, our results suggest that feedback plays a crucial role in galaxy evolution, with significant implications for theoretical models and future observations of galaxy evolution and halo mass. We evaluated the accuracy of novel photodetectors and automated photometric cameras by assessing their capabilities in aerosol assessments through the analysis of clear skies. These assessments rely on the scrutiny of sunset and sunrise colors, which are influenced by the effects of aerosols in the atmosphere. By utilizing standard photometric filters, we discovered that certain detectors, specifically those with broad red filters, can determine the aerosol optical depth with remarkable precision, achieving a high level of agreement with reference values and outperforming previous aerosol measurement methods in the region. Furthermore, we found that automatic, specially designed photometric cameras can accurately determine the aerosol optical depth and particle properties with minimal human intervention, showcasing their potential to contribute significantly to local aerosol monitoring networks. These innovative detectors and cameras can significantly enhance aerosol measurement operations, resulting in vital inputs for atmospheric modeling and environmental monitoring systems. Additionally, they can also facilitate the expansion of aerosol monitoring networks, especially in areas lacking such systems, thus providing valuable data for air quality management and environmental policy decisions. Lastly, we also discovered that these novel detectors can effectively operate without supplemental illumination, even at very low solar elevation angles, which could provide valuable insights into nocturnal aerosol layers and turbidity levels in the atmosphere. This could potentially lead to the detection of aerosol layering and other complex atmospheric phenomena. We also explored the feasibility of utilizing these detectors to determine the angular distribution of aerosols and assess the turbidity of the atmosphere, which could provide valuable insights into cloud properties and the overall state of the atmosphere. These findings pave the way for the widespread application of these automated systems in aerosol monitoring networks around the world, thereby significantly improving our understanding of atmospheric conditions. Moreover, we also observed that these novel detectors can effectively detect the effects of urban aerosols and other local air pollution sources, which could guide local air quality management initiatives and provide valuable data for environmental policy decisions. We also discovered that these detectors can effectively track the seasonal changes in aerosol particle properties, which could provide essential inputs for modeling and understanding atmospheric processes in the region. We also found that these novel detectors can effectively detect the effects of biomass burning and other types of aerosol sources, which could provide valuable data for fire detection and environmental monitoring in the region. Finally, we also observed that these detectors can effectively operate at high altitudes, which could provide valuable insights into atmospheric conditions at higher elevations and even in other regions. We introduce the GGLasso Python package, which enables the efficient computation of various Graphical Lasso estimators on both dense and sparse data formats. The GGLasso package offers a flexible framework for tuning multiple regularization parameters and choice selection, including Cross-Validation, Akaike Information Criterion, and Minimum Description Length within the Graphical Lasso framework. We demonstrate the GGLasso package's utility through two synthetic case studies and one real-world data analysis, showcasing its capability to handle large-scale sparse and dense data with rapid computational speed. We highlight the GGLasso package's capabilities and provide guidance on its implementation to promote reproducibility in future studies. Furthermore, we emphasize the GGLasso package's potential to address real-world data analysis challenges associated with heterogeneous data, diverse choice correlations, and time-series data complexities. The GGLasso Python package is freely accessible via PyPI and GitHub for community use. Due to technical issues, there is no abstract for arXiv:2102.10351. Theoretical models suggest that disk photoevaporation and magnetohydrodynamic winds can significantly impact planetesimal depletion and the final mass of planets. These models predict a distinctive radio signal from the disk's ionized edge or wind bubbles, but the predicted intensity varies greatly depending on the model. To verify these predictions, we examined the disk of TW Hydrae using two different models for radio emission and took into account the detection limits of future high-resolution telescopes like the Next Generation Very Large Array. Under the photoevaporation model, we found that the disk's outer regions would produce the strongest signal at an frequency of about 1.3 GHz, while the magnetohydrodynamic wind model predicted a stronger signal at higher frequencies. Notably, the theoretical predictions of both models agree that the disk's inner and outer edges will produce similar signals, but this will only be distinguishable with high-resolution (less than 0.1") observations at low frequencies (less than 1 GHz). Ultimately, future high-resolution radio observations will be crucial in determining the role of these processes in disk evolution and planetary formation. Additionally, such observations will allow us to assess whether the disk's mass has been accurately estimated based on observations of its thermal emission. With the advent of next-generation telescopes, we will be able to directly evaluate the disk's dynamics and understand the mechanisms driving its mass loss. The results of these high-resolution radio observations will also provide valuable constraints for simulating the evolution of T Tauri stars and their surrounding disks through direct visual inspection. The findings of this study will be made available in an interactive format, allowing users to modify various parameters and see how they affect the predicted radio signals. The code used in this study is also publicly available at https://github.com/ivanromani/astro_python_tools.git, where users can access a range of useful functions for simulating the evolution of stellar and sub-stellar objects and their surrounding disks. For numerous speech processing applications, it's crucial to determine voice presence and identify pitch. Typically, machine learning methods are used for this purpose, but they require large amounts of labeled data and can be less effective when data is hard to find or obtain. This paper presents an innovative solution that relies on unlabeled data to create categories based on voice characteristics. Once categories are established, the study proposes a technique using Kalman filters to track changes in pitch over time, showing this method outperforms existing approaches by successfully locating pitch in every frame of a test audio dataset. This dataset was created using synthetic speech for ease of analysis. When using real speech from a different source, the results show only minor decreases in performance. The research offers a promising approach to tackle related challenges in speech identification without labeled data. This work has implications for tasks like automatically transcribing audio from old recordings or detecting speech within background noise. We introduce a new method, dynamically weighted inertial forward-backward (DWIFOB), to tackle a particular type of optimization problem that involves individual components having a forward and backward part. By leveraging the convexity of these components, DWIFOB is shown to resolve the optimization issue efficiently and sustainably, even in the presence of non-convexity up to a certain point, by leveraging the Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz (KL) property, and providing strong convergence guarantees beyond that threshold. Moreover, we apply DWIFOB to solve problems involving split monotone variational inequalities, split Feasibility regularized Non-Convex Quadratic Programming, and a model for keyword extraction. The algorithm's effectiveness is also demonstrated through numerical experiments conducted on real-world data. DWIFOB can be found at https://github.com/JulienArchipielago/DWIFOB. Keywords: forward-backward splitting, strong convergence, KL property, feasibility regularized non-convex quadratic programming, keyword extraction, numerical experiments. Despite significant progress in neural network optimization, finding ideal architectures remains challenging, with most improvements stemming from the inherent biases of prior research rather than an in-depth understanding of how different components affect performance. This study introduces a design-by-numbers approach to neural network architecture synthesis, leveraging AI to generate and evaluate various architectures based on their inherent properties, such as connectivity patterns and layer types. By utilizing a property-based representation, which captures the essence of an architecture in a concise and easily analyzable format, our method can generate and assess a vast number of possible architectures while maintaining transparency and interpretability. This synthesis technique is then utilized to conduct a comprehensive search for optimal architectures suited to fundamental regression and classification tasks. The results demonstrate that our method is capable of producing architectures with exceptional accuracy, which can also be easily understood through attribute-based feature selection. Furthermore, our synthesized architectures consistently outperform previously established benchmarks, showcasing their versatility and potential for real-world application. Finally, a demonstration of our architecture synthesis capabilities is available at https://neuralarchitectureexploration.github.io/demos/. In this research, we tackle the issues of limited bandwidth and spatial interference in millimeter wave communications by designing a novel encoding technique called Hybrid Encoding (HE). By combining HE with compressive sensing, we develop a method to efficiently create transmission signals for specific groups within a network. Our approach enables each node to produce a signal using a sub-set of available frequencies and spatial beams, thus reducing interference and increasing data transmission speed. By comparing our solution with existing alternatives, we demonstrate through simulations that HE leads to a substantial increase in overall network capacity while maintaining acceptable levels of error rates. Furthermore, HE's performance can be optimized by adjusting a single parameter, yielding excellent results even in complex network scenarios. Finally, we show that HE's advanced features do not compromise its efficiency by achieving a high level of spectral efficiency in single-group settings. Our findings provide a solid foundation for future research into more sophisticated mmWave systems. Moreover, the study's outcomes can be applied to other multi-carrier networks, further enhancing their capabilities. Finally, the code used for these simulations is publicly accessible at the specified link.

Extraction techniques are the primary methodological framework for addressing
the challenges associated with labeling data, particularly when working with large
datasets. However, when applied in Federated Learning, they can lead to issues of
data leakage and loss of model confidentiality. Our study presents a novel
approach, called Communication-Efficient Federated Extraction, which enables the
efficient exchange of encrypted local extraction models between the client and
server while maintaining model confidentiality. Through performance benchmarks and
real-world evaluations using the CoQA dataset, we demonstrate the feasibility
and efficiency of this method in practical Federated Learning scenarios. Moreover,
CIFE offers greater flexibility and security compared to traditional local data
extraction, even allowing for the computation of tokenized data representations
on the server side. Furthermore, CIFE's security features can be adapted for use
in other Federated Learning methods. The source code for this project is available
on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/alexander-schulz/cife.

A novel approach to managing distributed computing systems is through Name Data Networking (NDN), which enables direct communication between services via named data objects, and simultaneously leverages local resources at multiple nodes. To achieve this, we develop strategies for dynamic online resource allocation that maximize overall system performance under specific constraints. Our specific research focuses on mobile ad-hoc networks where local computing resources and wireless connectivity vary, and we apply two different methods - Lagrange Multipliers and Prioritized Bandwidth Allocation. Through simulation-based evaluation, we compare these strategies against existing approaches, and the results indicate substantial improvements in system efficiency and quality of service. Furthermore, by analyzing the computational complexity of these methods, we identify suitable scenarios for their implementation. Ultimately, the trade-offs between system performance, resource utilization, and complexity are discussed. Experimental data shows that traditional methods fall short in managing distributed systems within mobile ad-hoc networks, whereas our proposed algorithms excel in such environments. Interestingly, the complexity of these systems often surpasses the capability of current state-of-the-art resource management techniques like Dynamic Voltage Isolation (DVI). Our research addresses this challenge by introducing an efficient online resource allocation method that achieves near-optimal results. Our contribution is two-fold: Firstly, we establish the optimal framework for resource management in ad-hoc networks. Secondly, we introduce a practical solution that can be implemented in real-time. Our findings have significant implications for managing local resources in NDN-based computing systems and can be applied to various scenarios beyond mobile ad-hoc networks. The code for reproducing our results is available at https://github.com/ahmed-omar/NDN-local-computing-coordination. Future research will focus on extending these ideas to more complex environments. Given the growing reliance on mobile local computing, our research has the potential to significantly impact the development of NDN-based distributed systems. By applying our methods, we can enhance the performance of existing software and leverage local resources more efficiently. Our approach can be applied to various scenarios beyond mobile ad-hoc networks, such as IoT, vehicular networks, and other environments with dynamic connectivity patterns. To validate our findings, we employed a realistic simulation environment using OpenNSL and PyNDN. The code for these simulations is available at https://github.com/ahmed-omar/NDN-local-computing-coordination. Future research will focus on exploring other applications of our research. We examine the exponential stability of the Euler-Bernoulli beam's extended movement on a star-shaped graph, proving that uniqueness of the optimal solution occurs and deriving both internal and external exponential stability indicators. Additionally, we provide numerical evidence to support our findings. Moreover, our investigation offers a practical solution to the Ritz method for this specific type of beam structure. The study enhances existing research on stability indicators by broadening its applicability beyond straight lines to more intricate star-shaped structures. All necessary technical details are included in two appended annexes. In particular, Annex I discusses crucial mathematical concepts, such as the inverse Holder inequality and the Bessel inequality, along with their practical implications, while Annex II presents a detailed analysis of the Ritz method's efficiency in predicting the stability indicators of this particular beam configuration. The research aims to contribute to the development of stability indicators that can be easily calculated and applied in real-world scenarios. Furthermore, it seeks to facilitate further research on stability in more complex systems and to inspire innovations in materials engineering with potential high-tech applications. Lastly, the research aims to promote the teaching of functional analysis in physics curricula through the practical example of this beam structure. The text is written in a didactically suitable style for undergraduate or graduate students in physics. Utilizing density functional theory and the 16-N rule for p-electron systems, the electronic configurations of CdTl$_4$Te$_3$ and HgTl$_4$Te$_3$ were determined. As first-time predictions in literature, they exhibit characteristics of a unique type of topological insulator with a large band gap, featuring hexagonal structure and belonging to the P-6m2 space group. Calculations showed that these compounds have a large band gap of approximately 3 eV, and are stable with an analysis of their formation energies. Furthermore, they display unusual chemical bonding between atoms, including the presence of Tl-Te and M-Te bonds in both compounds, as well as van der Waals interactions between Hg and Tl atoms in HgTl$_4$Te$_3$. These properties make CdTl$_4$Te$_3$ and HgTl$_4$Te$_3$ potential materials for spin-based information technology. (C) 2024 The Author(s). We develop an approach to learn effective utility functions from sample data in multi-objective optimization, allowing for incorporation of prior knowledge into the utility function. Our approach, utilizing evolutionary algorithms for utility function optimization, is demonstrated on two practical problems: designing multi-component proteins and finding MOGA-like trade-off surfaces. Diverse utility functions can be learned with our approach, yielding distinct Pareto-frontier approximations, including instances that incorporate prior knowledge and achieve better outcomes. Our results show that these optimized utility functions yield improved results in reinforcement learning and when applied to problems with available prior knowledge. Recent research has demonstrated that reinforcement learning agents are susceptible to various forms of adversarial attacks. Most existing studies have focused on targeting policies utilizing temporal information, but our research reveals that attacks on reinforcement learning can occur more easily when policies disregard time. By proposing a novel method of training an attacker, we show that policies lacking time-sensitive information can be effectively compromised. The complexity of our attack model is reduced, making it more feasible to carry out unauthorized actions against these agents. The success of our attack model is confirmed through experiments conducted on reinforcement learning agents trained for tasks such as Montezuma's revenge and lunar lander in the OpenAI Gym environment. Furthermore, we provide the developer with guidelines on how to strengthen their reinforcement learning model against unauthorized attacks. The impact of our attack is measurable, with the attacker successfully carrying out 90% of attacks against reinforcement learning models trained for a lunar lander task that land safely on the moon. Additionally, the attacker successfully compromises 100% of reinforcement learning models trained for a Montezuma's revenge task that collect over 1,000 points. Our research involves exploring a 2D periodic crystal structure featuring a rhombic lattice, where the symmetry of the lattice is generated by a non-symorphic group, resulting in the appearance of Dirac points at the edges of its Brillouin torus. By introducing strain into the system, we demonstrate the adjustment of its band structure, ultimately transforming the Dirac points into corner states that persist along specific lines in the momentum space. Additionally, we investigate other mechanisms capable of modulating the Dirac points, including twist angle variation and shear strain. With the application of strain, the system can transition between topological and non-topological states, thereby enabling the tuning of its band structure. Such a property could contribute to the development of novel quantum devices, including those utilizing strained materials to create non-Abelian excitations. Furthermore, we outline potential avenues for experimental realization by comparing our findings with those of a strained graphene sample. Lastly, we discuss the implications of our study on the band structure modifications resulting from structural strains in 2D materials. Our theoretical framework employs the tight-binding method and density functional theory to analyze the electronic properties of the strained rhombic lattice. These findings are expected to inspire research into strained quantum materials with exceptional properties, thereby advancing quantum technology. In risk-sensitive reinforcement learning (RL) based on the entropy penalty method, we investigate non-stationary environments where policies adapt to changing dynamics without assuming knowledge of the environment's structure or its non-stationary nature. We then develop an algorithm that achieves a regret bound of O(√(T log T)) within non-stationary environments and O(T^0.39) in stationary settings, showcasing its near-optimal performance. We also introduce a novel identification approach that adapts to changing dynamics, allowing it to separate environmental changes from non-stationary dynamics and providing statistical guarantees for policy transfer and dynamic regret assessment. Additionally, we present a design that separates risk sensitivity and non-stationarity, leading to improved performance and a simpler implementation. We validate our approach through numerical simulations and examine their theoretical implications. Notably, our results indicate that non-stationary RL algorithms can achieve optimal performance in non-stationary environments while also performing well in stationary settings, and that risk sensitivity can improve transfer results by encouraging exploration. Furthermore, our work demonstrates the practical utility of non-stationary RL in real-world scenarios, and that non-stationary environments can be identified and exploited through reinforcement learning methods. Finally, we show that non-stationary and risk-sensitive RL can be decoupled, leading to improved performance and simpler algorithms. Overall, our research contributes novel solutions to non-stationary RL in risk-sensitive settings, offering improved theoretical performance and practical applications that outperform existing methods. Moreover, our work presents an original framework that separates environmental non-stationarity, leading to enhanced adaptability and innovative RL designs. Lastly, we present a new paradigm for non-stationary and risk-sensitive RL that can be decoupled, resulting in more efficient algorithms. Multilingual individuals, having a command of two or more languages, are prevalent across four distinct categories according to their language use patterns: personal, social, domain-specific, and regional. This research aims to explore the patterns of language usage in multilingual environments and their underlying factors to better comprehend the requirements for natural language processing. Additionally, it highlights the advantages and difficulties of code-mixed NLP in comparison to monolingual NLP. We also identify key considerations for developers when designing NLP applications for multilingual users, taking Indian context code-mixed data-based NLP applications as a case study. We hope this study will facilitate the creation of more accessible and inclusive NLP services for millions of multilingual individuals worldwide. This article is an extended version of our initial input paper, presented at the 2021 International Conference on Advances in Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning. This article was initially published in the Proceedings of International Conference on Advances in Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning (ICAPRML '21).

In the field of biomedicine, graph depiction is crucial for conveying complex biological and medical relationships effectively, enabling healthcare professionals and researchers to grasp the underlying principles intuitively. Graph depiction serves as a visual tool with diverse applications across medicine, including clinical decision-making, education, and the communication of research findings to stakeholders. Despite its significance, graph depiction poses technical challenges, such as its subjective nature and the difficulty in evaluating its effectiveness. This study leverages deep learning techniques to develop an automated approach for creating graph depictions that outperform traditional manual methods, according to expert assessments, and achieves state-of-the-art results in benchmark evaluations. Furthermore, our findings highlight the potential for graph depictions to facilitate knowledge sharing among experts through successful representation of intricate biological and medical concepts. The implementation details and associated resources are available on GitHub at https://github.com/GraphDepiction/ and will be demonstrated at ICDM 2021 during an oral presentation. The graph depiction models have been integrated into the Cytoscape platform for widespread accessibility. Cytoscape can be accessed at https://cytoscape.org/. Research-based examples and expert-annotated datasets are available at https://graphdepiction.shinyapps.io/. Additionally, pre-trained models can be obtained via the Cytoscape plugin at https://cytoscape.org/plugins/gd/. Our team welcomes collaborations and can be reached via [kostas.gk@gmail.com](mailto:kostas.gk@gmail.com).

Our Graph Information Calculator method enables the calculation of differential privacy for any graph function that involves node or edge content, which can be integrated into a Privacy Advisor tool to provide personalized recommendations for users on how to set their privacy boundaries effectively when running such algorithms. Our experimental results demonstrate that our tool effectively identifies situations where graph content exposes sensitive user information and offers practical suggestions to maintain privacy while still producing accurate results. Our research addresses the limitations of current research and offers a content-based privacy framework that can be applied across multiple domains. Ultimately, our goal is to make graph privacy more approachable and provide users with simple, effective privacy solutions. Our system will be publicly available soon.

We examine two models, quantum purity and probabilistic purity, that conceal the true nature of items. Within the context of quantum purity, an individual may only measure a mixture of states, whereas in probabilistic purity, an item is either a valuable object with limited significance or discarded junk. Both models can represent approximate or precise characteristics but raise separate concerns regarding overestimation of measurement accuracy and optimal resource allocation due to the uncertainty of outcomes. We investigate these issues in more detail and explore potential solutions. Furthermore, we compare these models to the fundamental principles of scarcity and uncertainty, highlighting their differences and potential benefits. By refining our understanding of how people perceive and interact with objects, we hope to gain insights into broader societal issues related to resource management. Ultimately, our analysis suggests that addressing the inherent limitations of these concealment models is crucial to make informed decisions about how to utilize available resources effectively. The CP2K program package, often seen as an indispensable tool in atomistic simulations, highlights its capabilities particularly in carrying out ab-initio molecular dynamics through the application of the Car-Parrinello method's latest advancements. It then delves into current developments in low-scaling, massively parallel eigenvalue solvers and post-Hartree-Fock computations. The talk concludes by outlining future roadmap priorities that are anticipated to significantly boost the program's performance across a wide array of hardware platforms. These enhancements include but are not limited to improvements in linear solver techniques, the adoption of the Binary Neural Network method and the integration of the Generalized Polynomial Action Minimization algorithm. It is anticipated that through these improvements the program will be able to efficiently tackle problems involving the quantum motion of very large molecules. Additionally, efforts to make the program more user-friendly are being made via the development of the Trajectory Pallet, a collection of Python tools designed to streamline the analysis of CP2K trajectories. This pallet facilitates tasks such as the classification, storage and sharing of simulation data, along with the creation of visualizations and research reports. The integration of the program and pallet is then demonstrated through a concrete example, specifically in the simulation of the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein's surface region. This region, comprising of highly dynamic and flexible surface loops, poses a significant challenge to current simulation methods but is crucial in understanding viral antigenicity and receptor binding sites. The trajectory pallet's tools are then used to showcase its capabilities in analyzing CP2K trajectories, with the ultimate goal of enabling collaborative simulations that combine the efforts of various research groups. These collaborative simulations are anticipated to significantly advance our understanding of biomolecular systems, ultimately leading to breakthroughs in translational research and biotechnology development. In conclusion, the enhanced CP2K program, along with the supporting tools within the trajectory pallet, are poised to significantly contribute to the fields of atomistic simulation and structural biology as we approach the era of exascale supercomputing. This contribution is not only seen in efficiently harnessing the computational power of future supercomputers, but also in shedding new light on long-standing open questions in biomolecular physics. However, existing methods have primarily focused on single products with clear aspects, while overlooking cases involving multiple products sharing the same aspect or having sparse domains. To address this, we introduce a cooperative recommendation method tackling multi-sparse-domain challenges through a unified aspect-based framework. Initially, we utilize a proprietary neural network to capture users' preferences for shared aspects across products and their respective domains. Next, we employ a shared aspect-based model to learn users' preferences for product-specific aspects, while considering potential sparsity in domains. Lastly, a collaborative model aggregates aspect-based preferences to generate comprehensive aspect preferences, ultimately enabling the recommendation of cooperative products. Experimental evaluations on real-world data substantiate our method's superiority over existing approaches in covering user preferences and enhancing recommendation quality. Additionally, our method is capable of providing more accurate aspect-based user profiles with improved readability. Notably, it can handle sparse-domain challenges without requiring manual intervention. Overall, our method offers a versatile aspect-based solution for cooperative recommendation in real-world scenarios. The source code will be publicly available.

This research introduces an innovative neural network framework known as CICL-GNN, an approach that utilizes chance and differential equations to learn hidden variables through the analysis of observational data paired with a chance and differential equation model, despite the presence of noise. The method's effectiveness is showcased in two fundamental tasks: identifying latent structures in relational data and uncovering hidden variables in continuous observation records. Furthermore, the framework is also adapted to tackle the solution of stochastic differential equations, with the aim of performing variable selection in their equilibrium probability distributions. The results from these experiments highlight the efficacy of CICL-GNN, as it consistently outperforms existing graph neural networks in all tested applications. monotone optimization. The proposed stabilization techniques demonstrate

underpinnings for the use of stabilization techniques in monotone optimization. 
Given its broad applicability, this research can benefit multiple domains, such

preservation property and the Lipschitz-{\alpha} property. Three concrete

recovery. Finally, this research highlights potential areas of application

In this study, we derived key estimates for solutions of the 3D non-homogeneous Navier-Stokes equations given specific initial conditions with high periodicity. Notably, given a sufficiently low regularity of the initial velocity field relative to $k^{-\alpha}$ in frequency space, where $\alpha$ can range from $1/3$ to $1$, we demonstrated that the solution's velocity field and associated pressure remain smooth across all frequencies within a finite period of time. This outcome is particularly significant as it implies that the solution remains smooth until a non-linear instability phenomenon emerges, where the solution's frequency spectrum becomes infinitely steep. This research builds upon previous work by Kato and Kowalczyk-Mazzullo, providing additional insights into the behavior of solutions with initial conditions characterized by low regularity. Furthermore, our findings offer a fresh perspective on the frequency-dependent properties of solutions in the non-homogeneous setting. To achieve this, we employed a modified approach, incorporating the maximum metric to analyze the frequency response of solutions, which may have standalone value in the broader context of partial differential equations. This approach also facilitated a more streamlined proof of the non-homogeneous version of the Cauchy problem's well-posedness, a crucial concept in fluid dynamics. This research is an extension of our previous work, where we explored similar themes in the homogeneous setting. A key problem in quantum computing is determining whether a quantum gate sequence produces a outcome with a probability less than or equal to a specified threshold. Our approach uses a classical verification process that runs in linear time with a linear memory requirement, as opposed to existing methods which have cubic time complexity but lower memory needs. This advancement brings quantum computing validation closer in line with traditional computing paradigms in terms of resource efficiency. Additionally, we have developed two novel algorithms for checking if a quantum gate sequence is properly implemented. One algorithm requires linear memory and runs in quadratic time, while the other uses polynomial memory and runs in linear time. Both algorithms make use of a new type of circuit counting method which enables efficient verification of complex quantum gate sequences. Furthermore, these algorithms have been adapted to work within faulty quantum computing frameworks where random errors may occur during the computation process. All of these algorithms have been thoroughly tested against challenging scenarios arising from quantum computing's underlying mathematical structure, a field known as operator algebra theory. This proof-of-concept integration between quantum and operator algebra frameworks provides a foundation for developing robust fault-tolerance testing tools in quantum computing. Finally, we have successfully integrated our verification tools into an existing interactive proof system known as Brarkus, which has been adapted to work with quantum computations and serves as a demonstration of the efficacy of these algorithms in real-world applications. This work provides a thorough evaluation of the underlying mathematical concepts and presents a new perspective on the interaction between quantum computing and operator algebra. This new research could have significant implications for understanding the development of supermassive black holes in galaxies. A massive black hole, specifically those with masses greater than one million times that of our sun, found in a relatively small galaxy like Leo I defies the conventional understanding that such black holes are typically found only in larger galaxies. The "wide binary test" is one of the most effective methods of determining whether gravity behaves as predicted by the generally accepted theory of general relativity or an alternative theory in their respective ranges. Wide binaries remain stable over long periods as their motion is dominated by their initial velocity and gravitational attraction, with general relativity and alternative theories producing different predictions in their late-stage orbits. 

We conducted a comprehensive analysis of 98 binary systems with known orbital properties and a range of masses, and found that both their early and late-stage behavior aligns with the expectations of general relativity, with any discrepancies in their mid-stage behavior being within the measurement errors. 

Our findings are consistent with previous studies, and we attribute the differences in measurement errors to the differences in the binary system properties, specifically the mass ratio and orbital period. 

We also found that the current measurement precision is not sufficient to detect potential deviations from general relativity, and that future surveys with higher precision are required to utilize these binary systems as effective tests of the gravitational theory. 

Our analysis also revealed that the wide binary system 30~UMi, which was previously considered as an alternative to general relativity, in fact aligns with the expectations of general relativity when taking into account its changing luminosity and mass loss. 

In summary, our study demonstrates that the wide binary test is a reliable method for verifying the validity of the generally accepted gravitational theory, and that future high-precision surveys will be essential in further exploring the range of the gravitational theory. 

Our analysis also highlights the importance of utilizing high-level celestial mechanics techniques to analyze these binary systems, and that the wide binary test offers unique opportunities to study the stellar evolution and behavior.

This interaction can lead to the transfer of momentum from one mode to another, with electron-phonon coupling being a key factor. When electrons couple with phonons, momentum is conserved through the involvement of a third entity, either another phonon in the case of momentum exchange or a photon in the case of radiation effects. This transfer of momentum can result in the non-conservation of energy under equilibrium conditions, yet becomes crucial for understanding dynamic transport properties and spin dynamics in the presence of phonons. This study aims to investigate momentum transfer processes and their impact on the dynamics of both electrons and spins, with a particular focus on the influence of electron-phonon coupling on electron dynamics and the effects of spin-phonon coupling on spin dynamics and the eventual emergence of persistent spin currents. The findings of this study will provide valuable insights into the dynamic interactions of electrons, spins, and phonons, thereby facilitating the design of nanodevices with tailored electronic and spin properties. The research also explores the possibility of generating robust persistent spin currents in metal and semiconductor systems with specific spin blocking properties. The study utilizes a multi-scale theoretical approach that integrates density functional theory, semi-classical Boltzmann transport, and time-resolved quantum transport to analyze dynamic electron-phonon and spin-phonon interactions and their impact on the temporal evolution of momentum, distribution functions, and local spin polarization. This research investigates the problem of location privacy in the spatio-temporal context, aiming to protect users' path data. A specific form of privacy policy is introduced, which measures the maximum risk of revealing a location data segment when a specified privacy standard is breached. The introduced privacy policy can be addressed through a computational optimization problem, however its high dimensionality poses a significant challenge. Two methods are proposed to tackle this issue, one by applying a binary representation and leveraging advanced signal processing techniques to compress the data, the other by formulating the problem as a stochastic optimization problem. Results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods in enhancing location privacy. Additionally, this research introduces a location privacy management framework, enabling users to make informed decisions when sharing location data and maintain a level of privacy. Experimental findings using real data validate the framework's functionality and users can adjust the system to meet their specific privacy needs. Furthermore, this research contributes to the field by providing a precise bound on the violation of location privacy policies when location data is shared. A location privacy design method is also presented, allowing system designers to create location privacy policies that align with users' preferences. This research is relevant to various fields such as epidemiology, transportation, and crowd monitoring where location data is often involved. This approach allows us to extend the CME (concentration of measure equation) from non-directed graphs to directed graphs with positive Ricci curvature. Our results incorporate elements from a wide range of theoretical frameworks, including convex geometry and stochastic processes, and provide a practical means for directing graphs to converge to convex structures statistically. Furthermore, we provide functional and probabilistic CME formulations that offer insights into the behavior of directed graphs and explore their connections with non-directed graphs. Ultimately, our findings offer insights into the relationships between heat diffusion, directed graphs, and convex geometry. Examples and simulations have also demonstrated the practical applications of our theories. Lastly, our work has also revealed novel connections between stochastic processes and convex geometry that may be of value more broadly. Recent research has demonstrated the effectiveness of Pre-trained Models in handling code-mixed texts, however they often overlook the significance of switching points within these texts. This paper presents PESTO, an innovative Pre-trained Model that incorporates switching point information through two novel components: a Switching Point Enhanced Embedding table and a Positional Encoding module. The model optimizes token representation by leveraging contextual switching point information, while also enhancing attention pooling by incorporating relative positional encoding among mixing languages. Experimental evaluations on two substantial code-mixed datasets (CMD and CTS) reveal PESTO's superiority over existing Pre-trained Models in terms of both task-specific fine-tuning and zero-shot translation performance. Furthermore, the study highlights the importance of targeting switching points through enhanced embedding, as well as the positive impact of relative positional encoding on the model's overall performance. The findings suggest PESTO's potential to serve as a valuable starting point for Natural Language Processing tasks involving code-mixed texts. The model's source code is accessible via a GitHub repository at https://github.com/DeepTechAI/PESTO.

Utilizing density functional calculations with the inclusion of spin-orbit coupling, a comprehensive study has been conducted on the electronic structure, isotope effect, critical temperature, and critical pressure of the H$_{3}$S hydride from 150 to 250 GPa. A distinctive van Hove singularity (VHS) was located along the Fermi surface at increasing pressure, with its emergence coinciding with enhanced superconductivity and high critical temperatures. A VHS on one of the three hydrogen bands persists throughout the pressure range examined, with its intensity also present on the sulfur band at higher pressures, indicating that the VHS is crucial to the superconducting properties of H$_{3}$S. A VHS-driven isotope effect was observed, with the VHS-related density of states at the Fermi level serving as the key factor influencing the critical temperature. Additionally, the VHS was found to underlie the pressure dependence of the critical temperature, with the VHS-related critical pressure being significantly higher than expected. Overall, these findings underscore the pivotal role of the VHS in the superconductivity of H$_{3}$S and highlight its importance for understanding the physics of this and other multi-hydrogen and high-pressure compounds. While the average effect itself is unambiguous, determining the magnitude of its counterparts often poses statistical challenges. Fisher's intent was to highlight the importance of his average effect in the context of Mendelian inheritance patterns, specifically focusing on the interactions between genetic factors, their intermediate mechanisms (such as the Law of Segregation), and the ultimate expression of those factors (such as phenotypes). Machine learning models often face a problem known as statistical bias, which is particularly challenging in scenarios like semi-supervised learning on decentralized networks, where there's a lack of labeled data and heterogeneous training samples. When personalization is required, this issue is compounded by the fact that models may make inconsistent predictions on data from different users. This study addresses the issue of statistical bias in federated semi-supervised learning by proposing a new framework that minimizes personalization inconsistencies. Initially, we develop a new objective function that combines supervised and semi-supervised learning under centralized and decentralized settings. We then establish that optimizing this function reduces personalization inconsistencies, and can be effectively handled through stochastic gradient descent. Additionally, we provide a stopping criterion that prevents overfitting and ensures consistent predictions across users. This approach is validated through experiments on synthetic and real-world data, where it outperforms existing solutions in terms of prediction accuracy and personalization consistency. The code for this paper is publicly available at https://github.com/zhaozh/AmbiFedSSL.

The QQN comprises a series of quantized neurons that work in unison, allowing it to approximate the Q-function with precision. Utilizing tools from empirical process theory and entropy, we establish a central stochastic estimate for the Q-function, which serves as the objective function that the QQN method strives to minimize. Furthermore, we introduce a regularization technique known as post-quantization regularization (PQR) that enhances the QQN method's ability to generalize effectively, even when operating in high-dimensional environments. PQR achieves this by reducing the impact of overfitting through regularization, which in turn facilitates reliable policy implementations. PQR's efficacy is further underscored by our discovery that it translates to an L1 penalization effect on the Q-function itself. To solidify our claims, we conduct a series of experiments that showcase the performance of the QQN method, both with and without PQR, in a diverse range of games, including complex multi-player games like poker. To better understand patterns in an emergency department (ED), we analyzed treatment times using a reaction curve model, which represents how quickly staff respond to arriving patients. By averaging this reaction curve across multiple time points, we identified trends over time, discovering in the process a method to estimate the standard deviation of treatment times. Our results show that treatment times in the ED followed an initial non-linear pattern which eventually became linear as the department became busier, indicating a capacity beyond which further increases in patient volume would lead to treatments taking longer to complete. 

Key findings from our study include:
- Treatment times in the ED initially decreased as patient volume increased, but this improvement eventually reversed as the department became excessively busy.
- Average treatment times in the ED took around 7-10 hours to stabilize after the department's opening.
- Treatment times became more spread out as patient volume increased.
- Treatment durations in specific treatment areas within the ED exhibited varying patterns when compared to the overall ED.
- Treatment times in the ED were more unpredictable than previously estimated in existing research. 

To confirm our observations, we conducted statistical tests and found that treatment times followed a specific statistical distribution, commonly known as the Pareto distribution. Our analysis provides insights for decision-makers on how to effectively manage the ED and make informed decisions based on our findings. 

To illustrate the practical applications of our analysis, we used historical data from an ED to simulate how treatment times would change in different scenarios. Our results show that increasing the number of doctors and nurses by 10% would reduce average treatment times by around 8%. Furthermore, strategies to speed up treatment completion, such as implementing new technologies, could lead to significant improvements in patient care. 

In addition to these findings, we developed a method to estimate the optimal number of doctors and nurses required to achieve the best possible outcomes. Our results show that under normal operating conditions, the ED had the right balance of doctors and nurses, but during exceptionally busy periods, more staff would be needed to prevent treatment times from increasing. 

To validate our model's accuracy in predicting treatment times, we compared predicted and actual treatment times, discovering a positive correlation. Our analysis provides a foundation for developing data-driven algorithms to optimize the ED's operations and improve patient care.

This research focuses on the movement of electrons in modified SiMOSFETs (using a full 300mm CMOS process) in comparison to conventional MOSFETs, where significant enhancements have been observed. To achieve this, individual CMOS transistors were sourced and their performance evaluated after being detached from their original packages and etched to remove the back gate contact. Notably, high electron mobility was recorded at gate voltages between 0 and -3V, surpassing that of conventional MOSFETs by over 2 times. In particular, the maximum electron mobility at a gate voltage of -3V was 720 cm^2/Vs, while an increase of up to 1.5kV/cm was seen in mobility when the gate voltage rose from -3V to 0V. Building on these findings, the current flow in nFETs was modeled using ISE and MatCAD, where significant improvements in channel current were projected at high gate voltages. In summary, the modified SiMOSFETs displayed exceptional electron mobility at high gate voltages, indicating vast potential for these transistors to contribute to cutting-edge, high-performance electronic technology in the future. Additionally, the possibility of developing integrated high-mobility nFET and pFET CMOS circuits was explored. As an example, a simulated mobility gain of up to 4 times was achieved in the 802.11 ac standard when integrated in a CMOS technology. In another instance, a mobility gain of up to 2.5 times was achieved in the PA LNA unit of an LTE receiver when integrated in a CMOS technology. In summary, the integration of high-mobility nFETs in CMOS technology holds significant potential for developing highly efficient and high-performance electronic circuits in the future. Additionally, the developed technique has the potential to significantly enhance the performance of existing CMOS digital and radio frequency circuits by replacing pFETs with high-mobility nFETs. Graph Neural Networks have achieved significant success in multiple domains, but their effectiveness heavily relies on the quality of annotated data, which can be costly and time-consuming to obtain.  To overcome this limitation, researchers have developed methods to create artificial labels (pseudo-labels) for unmarked data using existing models, which can then be refined through repeated iterations.  Nevertheless, these pseudo-labels are often inaccurate and can introduce noise into the training process.  To improve the reliability of pseudo-labels, we introduce a new method called Informative Pseudo-Tagging (IPT), which only assigns pseudo-labels to data nodes with high annotation confidence, thereby reducing noise from unreliable pseudo-labels.  IPT utilizes a built-in classification module to assign pseudo-labels to data nodes and estimates annotation confidence through the predictive entropy of the classification output.  By comparing IPT to current state-of-the-art methods on three graph classification benchmarks, we demonstrate that our approach achieves superior performance with fewer iterations and improved robustness to noise.  Furthermore, IPT exhibits reduced computational complexity and memory requirements compared to existing methods.  To validate the effectiveness of IPT, we conducted two experiments: adding artificial labels to a semi-supervised task and simulating noisy labels in a supervised setting.  IPT outperformed the benchmarks in both experiments and showed improved robustness to noise.  The source code for IPT is available at https://github.com/zhaozhanyu/IPT. IPT is currently supported on PyTorch and TensorFlow.  We anticipate IPT to contribute positively to the research community by providing a versatile and efficient method for pseudo-labeling.  In the future, we plan to enhance IPT by incorporating more methods to filter data nodes for pseudo-label assignment.  We also expect IPT to be applied in more real-world tasks such as natural language parsing and social network analysis. Precise smoke removal in laparoscopic surgery videos is crucial for minimizing interference and ensuring a clear view for the surgeon to perform procedures safely and effectively.  We begin by examining how smoke detection in these videos is typically enhanced through image processing techniques, and then investigate the potential for pre-processing methods to improve smoke identification.  Specifically, we evaluate the utility of pre-processing laparoscopic videos through pre-conditioning, a process of modifying the color or tone of the images, and image enhancement, which involves adjusting the images based on pixel values.  Our analysis reveals that pre-processing can indeed contribute to the improvement of smoke detection, and we subsequently introduce a pre-processed pre-conditioning and enhancement-based method for smoke detection, which surpasses the performance of existing techniques.  This work has far-reaching implications for laparoscopic surgery, emphasizing the significance of pre-processing in surgical video smoke removal for surgical safety. Recent advancements have led to increased interest in multivariate functional data, which has resulted in the development of functional Gaussian graphical models. On the other hand, leveraging stochastic processes as 'functions', Gaussian processes can be used to model random functions, which has implications for functional data analysis. Graphical Gaussian processes provide a framework for functional data that incorporates complex dependencies while allowing for the estimation of underlying graphs. This paper explores the relationship between graphical Gaussian processes and the specific case of GP(2) processes, which are connected to the x-bilinear model, and reveals a previously unnoticed equivalence with functional Gaussian graphical models, particularly those based on squared-exponential kernels and equipped with covariance matrices suited for functional data. This equivalence enables the transfer of functional data analysis tools to the realm of graphical Gaussian processes, which in turn has implications for the distribution of functional covariance matrices and related graph estimation problems. Our findings are substantiated through simulations and real-world applications drawn from the fields of neuroscience and systems biology. Ultimately, this research opens up new avenues for combining differential equation-based Gaussian processes and functional Gaussian graphical models to analyze complex, interconnected functional data. Compiling quantum circuits efficiently is crucial for achieving high performance on large-scale quantum computers. The current leading method, Variational Decomposition, excels at optimizing common circuits, but its efficiency severely declines when faced with circuits containing recurring patterns. In an effort to overcome this limitation, this paper introduces two innovative deterministic compilation techniques designed to handle circuits with recurring patterns: Direct mapping and Hybrid Approach. The Direct mapping technique significantly boosts compilation speed and efficiency by optimizing recurring patterns directly, without breaking them down into smaller components. The Hybrid Approach takes this a step further by combining the strengths of Variational Decomposition and Direct mapping, yielding superior results across a wide range of circuit architectures. The effectiveness of these techniques was rigorously tested against the industry-standard Azure Quantum's QSharp compiler and Variational Decomposition, with impressive results showing substantial time savings without compromising accuracy. The proposed techniques have far-reaching implications for optimizing quantum computing applications. Their stable performance and high efficiency make them ideal for general-purpose quantum compilers, while also paving the way for novel applications such as generating quantum circuits with specific characteristics. This dual structure is comprised of a graph representing the set of maximal ideals within a given orthomodular lattice, its subgraph derived from the dual of the original lattice's bounded below parts, and a further refined subgraph obtained from the dual of the original lattice's bounded above parts. These subgraphs are then combined into a single graph for the given orthomodular lattice, and a topological structure is applied to it to yield a new graph. This process is reversible, allowing the return to the original lattice from its geometric graph representation. Additionally, this geometric framework enables the translation of lattice operations into graph-based operations, providing a new perspective on the underlying structure of orthomodular lattices. This geometric translation further enables the examination of certain properties of the lattices in terms of graph topology. Furthermore, we extend this geometric framework to include systems of maximal ideals within orthomodular lattices, which is analogous to the established connection between frames and simplicial complexes in the literature. In interior point methods (IPMs), where interior points are feasible solutions to nonlinear or convex optimization problems with equality constraints, subspace interior point methods (SIPMs) are a subclass that utilize subspace projections or approximations to the interior of the feasible region. When solving quadratic programs with a positive definite matrix, Krylov solvers like the Conjugate Gradient method are frequently employed for matrix inversions in IPMs and SIPMs. This paper introduces an innovative termination criterion for these solvers, grounded in the interior point methodology, which also considers (1) expected angular errors $\theta$ and (2) residual norms $r$. When either threshold is met, the algorithm halts; otherwise, it proceeds as usual. The proposed criterion is verified to be effective and functions independently of its underlying method, thus complementing existing halting criteria while providing enhanced adaptability to SIPMs that utilize gaseous search directions. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through its integration in RAPTL, a general-purpose SIPM code, which is then applied to solve a test set of 107 quadratic programs. The results indicate that the new criterion leads to a noticeable reduction, averaging 2.27% on standard hardware, in solver time at a cost of only 0.01% increased inner iterations. Furthermore, it enables SIPMs to exploit search directions that were previously considered useless, resulting in a 10.5% reduction in solver inner iterations. Quipper, a domain-specific language, enables efficient compilation of quantum circuit-based programs into multiple executable formats, including hardware-dependent low-level codes, high-level quantum algorithms, and interactive simulations within the quipper framework. The original Quipmer language serves as the starting point for translating quantum circuit-based programs in quipper, offering a modular and abstract specification of quantum hardware with virtual gates and circuits. However, the current Quipmer semantics incorporated within the quipmer framework is tied to specific assumptions about physical gate implementation, restricting portability across diverse quantum hardware configurations. This study introduces a new language, proto-quipper-m, designed as a direct evolution from quipmer, aiming to enhance portability through flexible and hardware-agnostic program writing. The proposed proto-quipmer-m language retains key features from quipmer while introducing dynamic gate application and circuit creation based on user-defined templates. To ensure a seamless transition between abstract hardware specifications and low-level circuit descriptions, the proto-quipmer-m language is complemented by a formal semantics, facilitating automatic code generation for simulations, algorithmic presentations, and low-level circuit descriptions. This study presents a formalization of the proto-quipmer-m language through a relational denotational semantics, enabling the interpretation of quipper programs as circuit families, compatible with the existing quipper framework. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates that the proto-quipmer-m language can be seen as a particular instance of the abstract quipmer semantics, effectively reflecting the evolution of quantum hardware configurations from abstract to low-level circuit descriptions. The findings of this study offer novel solutions for generating low-level circuit descriptions directly from the abstract proto-quipmer-m programs, potentially applicable to other quantum algorithms as well. The research outcomes may also contribute to future advancements in quantum hardware, potentially leading to breakthroughs in quantum algorithm design. The quipmer and proto-quipmer-m language specifications, along with their corresponding formalized semantics, are freely accessible through the co-implemented interactive theorem prover, quipmer4coq. The quipmer4coq tool allows for additional verification support, aiming to facilitate reliable program development within the quipmer framework. The resulting proto-quipmer-m language can enhance portability through flexible and hardware-agnostic program writing, contributing to improved quipper programs that can be seamlessly compiled into low-level circuit descriptions for simulations, algorithmic presentations, and high-level quantum algorithms. Assembling a complete genome from short, overlapping DNA sequences is a complex problem that becomes more tractable with the use of long-range sequencing data. Although this advancement increases the size of the input data, it also presents new opportunities for developing efficient assembly algorithms. One such algorithm utilizes a graph data structure to store the sequence overlaps and enables accurate genome reconstruction by identifying the most probable contiguous sequences. However, calculating contiguous sequences within this graph can be computationally intensive and may benefit from parallel processing. In this research, we introduce a new method to break down the contiguous sequence computation task into discrete components, which are then processed in parallel memory partitions to produce the complete sequence output. Our approach effectively leverages distributed-memory architecture and outperforms a previous serial algorithm by achieving speedup of up to 3.6 times using only 128 parallel processing units. Furthermore, when applied to a single 40-core CPU system, this method results in a noticeable reduction of the assembly timeline of up to 2.5 times. Additionally, we observed a direct correlation between the number of parallel processing units and the speedup achieved, which validates the efficiency of our distributed-memory parallel contig creation algorithm. Lastly, using the same architecture, we achieved a 4.1 times speedup in the overall genome assembly process. These findings are further substantiated by a detailed analysis of the assembly graph's characteristics and the impact of parallel processing on the genome assembly output. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the feasibility and effectiveness of applying parallel processing techniques to enhance the genome assembly process. Our experimental investigation employs the ISOLDE facility at CERN via a multi-parameter setup, combining in-gas and in-trap measurements, to study the magnetic dipole moments of the Germanium isotopes with odd mass numbers between 62 and 70. We determined the nuclear properties and collective motion characteristics for these isotopes, revealing that the 69Ge-69 nucleus exhibits unique ground states. Our data, supplemented by large-scale shell-model calculations, suggests that the 69Ge-69's ground state has an unusual structure with no collective deformation, but rather a symmetric shape characterized by a shifted 40Ne core and coupled 29Si and 20Ne neutrons and 17Ne protons. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the 69Ge-69's single-particle configuration is distinct from its neighboring Germanium isotopes, occurring at an exceptionally isolated instance, thus providing significant insights into the fine details of the nuclear landscape near N = 40 and refuting previous theoretical predictions of collective deformations in this region. We also report the measured magnetic dipole moments for 63Ge-31, 65Ge-31, and 67Ge-31 and the 71Ge-31 moment, with a newly calculated 69Ge-69 moment. Our data for 67Ge-31 and 71Ge-31 corrects and normalizes previous measurements, offering comprehensive nuclear property data for Germanium up to mass number 71. Our study contributes valuable information towards refining the nuclear mass model and shell-model interaction for this region, thus facilitating future experimental investigations. Additionally, our research may contribute to a deeper understanding of the nuclear structure and could have implications for the development of new targets and nuclear beams in geodesic experiments. Monte Carlo simulations are becoming increasingly essential in various fields of physics, enabling researchers to obtain numerical approximations of systems that cannot be solved exactly by computers. To tackle diverse problems across different domains, researchers have developed and proposed numerous algorithms, often without considering their computational implications, leading to a lack of transparency and reproducibility. To address this issue, the concept of "flows" has been introduced as a unified framework to represent and document these algorithms, promoting reproducibility and facilitating contributions from the broader community. In this review, we will outline the core elements of flows and illustrate their application in lattice field theory using complex systems as examples. Additionally, we will highlight publicly available tools and platforms that can be utilized to standardize flows and enhance algorithmic research. Furthermore, we will discuss future directions and potential applications of flows within the context of lattice field theory. Lastly, we will invite readers to explore the associated documentation and contribute their knowledge to the field.

In natural language processing, text-to-SQL translation has gained significant attention for enabling the translation of spoken language into SQL queries, but tackling ambiguity and domain-specific challenges proves to be difficult, particularly when little training data is available for a particular domain. This research proposes a novel, multi-part approach to overcome these difficulties. Firstly, it employs pre-trained language models to generate SQL queries in a familiar domain. Secondly, it utilizes the generated SQL to guide the translation in an unfamiliar domain aided by an additional auxiliary task. This auxiliary task involves predicting the generated SQL's meaning in an unfamiliar domain. Experimental results demonstrate that this method surpasses current domain-agnostic solutions and exhibits comparable results with domain-specific models regarding accuracy and naturalness. Notably, it achieves an 88.4% execution rate that rivals a model with access to an additional 50k dataset. This breakthrough is largely due to its ability to mitigate ambiguity in an unfamiliar domain. All code and data used in this research can be accessed at https://github.com/whaiwhai/End2End_Cross_Domain_T2SQL.

The High-Dimensional Rank Lasso (HDRL) model offers a significant improvement over the Lasso method in dealing with strong correlations among variables. However, solving HDRL represents a challenging nonlinear optimization task, especially in high-dimensional settings. Existing solutions primarily rely on discarding certain variables based on correntropy-based rankings and then applying conventional optimization techniques, which can lead to suboptimal solutions if certain variables are discarded prematurely. Another major limitation is that these methods are only suitable for small to medium-sized datasets. In this research, we present a new algorithm that builds on the idea of adaptive sieving by dividing problem-solving into distinct stages, each targeting a subset of variables. Our algorithm is designed to be highly adaptable, allowing it to selectively include or exclude variables at each stage based on its marginal contribution. Experimental results demonstrate that our algorithm not only overcomes the dimensional constraints of existing solutions but also yields improved precision compared to state-of-the-art methods in high-dimensional settings. This investigation focuses on both experimental and theoretical aspects to uncover the relationship between convective entropy production and system instability.
