Machine learning algorithms are increasingly being utilized for treating imbalanced data by generating biased predictions, yet their applications are restricted when compared to traditional approaches such as logistic regression, which can produce probability estimates crucial for variance estimation in difference-in-mean estimators.  By combining machine learning predictions with the inverse probability weighting method, an augmented estimator is created which offers improved efficiency relative to traditional approaches, though it suffers from increased variance due to additional bias introduced by the machine learning component,  beyond what is seen in traditional logistic regression based methods.  Through the application of a neural network to predict predictions made by a logistic classifier, a form of standardized augmented IPW is achieved, which successfully reduces the additional variance introduced by the machine learning component, thus resulting in improved efficiency when compared to both naive machine learning and traditional logistic regression based methods.  Our results are further validated through empirical tests on real-world datasets.  Notably, while our method is primarily framed within the context of treatment and exposure, it is equally applicable to a wide range of imputation and targeting applications.  Code for our method is available at https://github.com/alexeygrigorev/sail.  Sail is an R package which standardizes augmented IPW with various machine learning algorithms.  It includes support for neural networks, random forests, gradient boosting machines and others.  It also features a graphical user interface for easy data exploration and estimation. A common strategy for modeling extreme events involves using intermediate data such as peak excess exceedances above a high threshold, and then combining this with location and scale parameters for a specific distribution such as the Gumbel or Frankel distributions. While this two-stage approach has been effective, it presents challenges in terms of posterior distribution computation and Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling. This paper introduces a modified method based on a different parameterization that directly works with the extreme values, and shows through simulation that it offers improved efficiency in sampling and easier computation than the traditional two-stage approach using intermediate data. The new method using a shifted and scaled parameterization for a Poisson process works effectively with both Gaussian and Pareto distributions, and is implemented through a simple Metropolis-Hastings algorithm. The results demonstrate that this approach leads to more precise estimates and a more efficient posterior distribution, and can also be used to estimate the probability of future exceedances. The approach is then tested with real data from the River Conwy in Wales. The code used in this research is available on GitHub at https://github.com/alexbowen/extremes_ppssp. A critical issue in testing a model's robustness against out-of-distribution (OOD) data lies in accurately categorizing and representing real-world OOD text varieties. While models can generally detect blatant OOD examples, such as foreign languages, they often falter against more subtle forms like domain-specific jargon or altered text modifications. However, there is currently a lack of consensus on categorizing and representing OOD text types. In response, we introduce a new dataset, Meta-Sat, comprising satellite images with diverse data sources and resolutions, alongside a new text-based OOD evaluation, where models must distinguish between specific text categories. Our results indicate that current models fall short in identifying less obvious forms of OOD data and that refining data augmentation and pretraining can enhance a model's OOD performance. Our work aims to facilitate further research on text-based OOD data and provide a unified benchmark for evaluating models' robustness against distinct data sources. You can access our dataset at https://github.com/0grig0/out_of_distribution.

In the field of combinatorial design theory, generalized convolutions represent an important concept that has been extensively studied, with numerous properties and patterns emerging from them. This research aims to identify new and distinct patterns that emerge from the generalized convolution of two integer sequences, $a$ and $b$, with specific characteristics, within the framework of the Fibonacci sequence where the latter sequence, $b$, has a fixed, varying length and is generated from the former sequence, $a$, through a repeated application of the Fibonacci substitution sequence, $\sigma$. All sequences considered within this study are non-negative and consist of integers that do not exceed 1. This paper presents an efficient algorithm for computing the generalized convolution of two sequences, $a$ and $b$, with the added constraint that sequence $a$ must also satisfy the modulo 2 congruence of 0, using the Multiplicative Generalized Convolution Algorithm (MGC). This algorithm offers a significant improvement over the traditional brute-force method, reducing computation time while enabling the discovery of new patterns in the Fibonacci sequence in a timely manner. Additionally, this paper showcases the feasibility of employing the MGC algorithm to compute the convolution of two sequences, $a$ and $\sigma(b)$, for which the brute-force method has been previously utilized. This research further includes a comprehensive examination of the computational complexity of the MGC algorithm and demonstrates that its runtime is directly proportional to $n^{1.5}$ when using a divide-and-conquer approach and proportional to $n$ when employing a bit-manipulation strategy, both of which are more efficient than the brute-force method. This study presents an extensive list of newly discovered patterns in the Fibonacci sequence, which were computed using the MGC algorithm at a length of $n=30$ and verified to be correct through manual verification at shorter lengths of 14 and 28. Furthermore, this research includes a comparison of the MGC algorithm with another algorithm, the Additive Generalized Convolution Algorithm (AGC), which demonstrates their equivalence in computing the convolution of two sequences, $a$ and $\sigma(b)$, with the added constraint that sequence $a$ must also satisfy the modulo 2 congruence of 0. This equivalence in computing the convolution of two sequences, $a$ and $\sigma(b)$, using both the MGC and AGC algorithms, which were previously known to be distinct, represents a groundbreaking finding in the generalized convolution theory. The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 sparked significant interest in the study of ultra-cool dwarfs, particularly due to its potential to offer insights into the formation and evolution of brown dwarfs. However, the current understanding of GJ 229B is limited by the uncertainty surrounding its spectral type, which has implications for the knowledge gap between the known T and Y dwarfs. To resolve this uncertainty, we employed the APOLLO retrieval code to analyze the spectral features of GJ 229B's emission spectrum, obtained from the Spitzer Space Telescope at 1.5 $\mu$m. By using a grid of atmospheric models that span a range of pressures, compositions, and thermal profiles, we were able to determine the most suitable model for the dwarf based on its best-matching CH$_4$ and H$_2$O absorption patterns. Our analysis revealed a spectral type of T5 and suggested the presence of hazes composed of tholins, as well as a possible pressure of 1-10 bar. This discovery led to the proposal of two possible formation scenarios for GJ 229B, which may be consistent with the presence of a surrounding disk or the dwarf's migration into its current orbit. Furthermore, our findings provided an estimate of the dwarf's mass, which lies within the range of 15-40 M$_{\odot}$. The implications of our results for the study of ultra-cool dwarfs are significant, as they offer new insights into the atmospheric composition and properties of the first known T-dwarf, GJ 229B. These findings also highlight the potential of future spectroscopic observations with the JWST and other advanced telescopes to expand our knowledge of brown dwarf physics. To achieve this goal, we have outlined a plan for the necessary follow-up observations required to confirm our retrieval's accuracy and further elucidate the atmospheric characteristics of GJ 229B and other similar objects. A double auction is the most commonly used trading system in financial markets, responsible for executing transactions worth trillions of dollars daily. Its effectiveness can be evaluated using the principles of price efficiency, where market prices are determined by the intersection of buyer and seller demand curves. This concept is theoretically grounded in general equilibrium theory. This study aims to expand this understanding by analyzing the behavior of market participants during times of crisis. Researchers developed a model to simulate price formation in real-time, combining theoretical foundations with cutting-edge machine learning algorithms. This combined approach, known as the fundamental-price model, leverages economic principles and statistical tools to improve price efficiency. When implemented in a tested market environment, the fundamental-price model outperformed traditional methods, resulting in reduced price fluctuations and more accurate market valuations. This innovation provides a framework for market regulators to assess the stability of financial markets during periods of high volatility. Furthermore, the fundamental-price model enables its integration into double auction trading systems, ensuring their continued stability and accuracy. This finding offers valuable insights to market managers and a method for market surveillance, as demonstrated through validated results presented in the study. The application of the fundamental-price model could serve as a template for governing the stability of financial markets affected by extreme events. This research examines the effectiveness of the Chambolle-Pock algorithm (CPA) in resolving the Moreau envelope for a combination of convex and nonexpansive functions. Although CPA is known to converge optimistically for certain nonexpansive processes, it falls short in certain nonexpansive scenarios. We address these shortcomings by deriving conditions that ensure CPA converges optimistically across all nonexpansive processes. Additionally, we propose an alternative method, derived from Bregman iterations, which shares similarities with CPA but achieves optimistic convergence for any nonexpansive process. We also introduce a simpler, nonparameterized algorithm to solve the same problem, which has a notable advantage of requiring only a single vector storage per iteration. We further extend our findings to address nonsmooth convex optimization, providing a simpler nonparameterized method that converges optimistically. Notably, our storage requirements are significantly lower than current methods, with our simplest nonparameterized algorithm needing only three vector storage spaces throughout its process. We also provide empirical evidence supporting our theoretical claims through numerical testing. Finally, we present an interesting application of our findings, which can be utilized in periodic decompositions and clustering problems. We believe our research offers valuable insights into nonsmooth optimization and clustering problems, while also introducing innovative solutions to these challenges. The code for our experiments is available at https://github.com/ivanolea/nonexpansive_convergence. A new approach to dynamic mode decomposition using kernel methods, called linear and nonlinear clarification optimization (LANDO), is developed within the context of kernel dynamic mode decomposition. LANDO is based on a few key assumptions regarding the structure of the system operator and is framed as an optimization problem that can be solved through stochastic gradient descent. The method is particularly effective in situations where the system operator acts nonlinearly on high-dimensional input variables and is subject to significant noise levels. The algorithm employs multiple techniques to reduce the computational complexity of large kernel matrix operations and can be executed in an online capacity, enabling real-time performance even when dealing with large datasets. The efficacy of the method is validated through a range of tests, including synthetic data simulations and applications to real-world datasets derived from experimental observations and remote sensing imagery. The results obtained from these evaluations indicate that LANDO is capable of accurately extracting relevant spatiotemporal features and outperforms dynamic mode decomposition and kernel dynamic mode decomposition in terms of robustness across varying data resolutions and noise levels. The code for LANDO is freely accessible via the repository https://github.com/krishnan-kaushal/lando_kernel_dmd. The repository also contains modified versions of the pydy library that incorporates support for the method in question. The method is described in detail in a recently published study (Krishnan et al., 2021). The objective of this research is to quantify the complexity and similarity of chess openings using large datasets from online chess communities, specifically examining how these concepts evolve over time. By employing a network approach to map out the relationships between openings and using a variety of statistical tools, such as clustering, information theory, and dynamic networks, our study reveals how chess players' strategies have changed over the past ten years and how different players analyze openings in terms of complexity. This study presents a novel approach for determining the mass and spin characteristics of millisecond pulsars by incorporating accretion into white dwarfs using advanced asteroseismology techniques, combining this with observations of pulsar systems that emit radiation in visible light, such as binary pulsar PSR J1713+7360, and pale dwarf stars like GD 358 and HB 21, to establish a universal set of fundamental parameters for these stars, including mass, radius, and internal composition. We employ the Shallow Water Method and the Maximum Entropy Method to analyze oscillation frequencies and perform constrained optimizations to determine the characteristics of these stars. We then use the location of these stars in the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram to refine our findings, specifically for GD 5015, where we calculate the helium mass fraction as 0.01. We apply our method to the pulsar-dwarf binary system PSR J1713+7360, and find that the mass of the dwarf, used as the initial mass for the pulsar, falls within the expected range for such systems, providing further evidence for the radio pulsar's spin characteristics, including its magnetic field strength, and the properties of the orbit, including eccentricity and the length of the orbit. Finally, our study underscores the importance of utilizing a diverse range of observational data to inform our understanding of stellar astrophysics. A thorough investigation into nonlocal properties of motion within the Lagrangian framework, applicable to systems of any higher order, is presented. Initially, a general nonlocal nonvariational problem is defined through discrete variables, then reduced to a corresponding local problem via a differential equation. Properties of nonlocal characteristics in both first-order (classical) and second-order dynamical systems are extensively examined, with the theory being further illustrated through relevant geometric examples. Finally, the findings are applied to construct closed nonlocal characteristics in conservative systems, thus paving the way for innovative solution approaches. In contrast to classical mechanics, these new methods offer additional degrees of freedom, potentially enabling more efficient solution evaluation and expansion problems. In addition to expanding existing results by M. Crampin et al., the study also explores nonlocal properties in the most fundamental case of first-order dynamical systems on a 2D-plane with smooth curves. This work has potential practical implications, including the adaptation of modern navigation technologies, which rely on nonlocal properties, to historical sailing methods involving the use of charts. Ultimately, the research contributes to expanding the repertoire of modern classical mechanics, enabling innovative approaches to solution evaluation and expansion problems. As a result, the study may influence the development of related fields, including modern navigation and control. Due to its theoretical nature, the research is presented with minimal reference to real-world examples, with three illustrative geometric examples provided to facilitate comprehension. The remainder of the document is organized as follows. In Section 2, a general nonlocal nonvariation problem is defined using discrete variables, with corresponding local problems derived from differential equations. In Section 3, properties of nonlocal characteristics in first-order dynamical systems are examined in detail, with additional analysis presented in Section 4 for second-order systems. The theory is then applied to construct closed nonlocal characteristics in conservative systems, as demonstrated in Section 5. Finally, in Section 6, the findings are adapted to explore nonlocal properties in first-order dynamical systems on a 2D-plane with smooth curves, before concluding with a discussion in Section 7. The supporting geometric examples are presented in Section 8. The research was initially presented at the XXVIII Autumn School on Geometric Methods in Physics in 2019. A key objective in understanding human motor control is to create algorithms that mimic efficient movement patterns in human beings. While current neural network-based methods can generate random movements that target specific points, they often require excessive trials and time to reach goals. To overcome this limitation, we suggest a method to drive movement learning by focusing on the movement's purpose. This purpose is represented as a metric that measures how a movement's progress aligns with the desired outcome, and when optimized, leads to better performance. Our study tests this idea using two realistic simulations of the human locomotion and reaching skills, and the results show that learning is significantly accelerated with this goal-oriented approach. Furthermore, the algorithm develops more practical and effective movement patterns that closely resemble real human movements, as observed in video recordings and scientific studies. Compared to traditional methods, our approach reduces the required number of trials by at least tenfold, while producing similar or better outcomes. Additionally, the movements generated with our method have similar patterns in muscle activation, joint angles, and torque as those recorded in real humans, which underscores the algorithm's ability to capture the underlying mechanics of motor control. Vibrant Poincaré symmetry is an extension of Poincaré symmetry obtained by boosting its spatial translations to higher rank. This enhancement yields a deformed mixture of Poincaré and Galilean algebras. Within a general framework, we derive deformed actions for gravity and general matter fields, specifically scalar and Yang-Mills fields, by applying the general concept of'symmetry boost' to established theories based on Poincaré symmetry. These actions are then analyzed within two contexts: as self-consistent theories within a specific regime and as deformations of Einstein's gravity and classical Yang-Mills theory. Furthermore, we explore potential links to Horndeski theories and related cosmological models. Lastly, we examine the implications of our findings for the galileon theory's deformed version, along with discussing open issues and potential areas for further research.

In visual navigation, successfully completing a task relies on effectively utilizing previously encountered objects or locations to guide forward movement.  The challenge lies in determining which memories to access and when to incorporate them into decision-making processes.  Current methods often integrate all acquired memories into state representations or utilize them through attention-based mechanisms that don't guarantee memories' impact on control actions.  We introduce MemoNav, an object-oriented memory system that addresses these concerns by selecting memories relevant to current objectives and storing them in working memory for infusion into action-planning processes.  MemoNav's ability to filter and manage memories enables it to outperform existing methods in visual navigation tasks.  Our research includes experiments that demonstrate MemoNav's ability to organize and prioritize memories, as well as real-world evaluations where it successfully navigates diverse environments.  By replicating human memory management, MemoNav, an integrated framework for perception-action systems, can serve as a guideline for developing more efficient memory-based robotic systems. The rapid proliferation of mobile devices necessitates the continuous evolution of cellular networks to meet increasing user demands for data and video content. This requirement has driven innovation in mobile communication systems, leading to the development of 5G through enhanced spectral and spatial efficiency, and is now pushing the boundaries of research in 6G technology. To achieve a seamless transition from 4G to 6G, it is crucial to understand the historical context and progress of cellular network evolution. This article delves into the origins and progress of cellular networks since the early 1980s, highlighting key advancements that paved the way for future growth. Building on past successes, researchers are working to address emerging challenges in future wireless networks, such as the relentless growth of mobile data, the need for pervasive and high-speed connectivity, and the increasing demand for communication, computation, and intelligence within everyday devices and objects. To meet these needs, future wireless networks will likely be characterized by ultra-reliable, adaptive, and integrated data communication, as well as advanced technologies such as terahertz frequency, nanotechnology, artificial intelligence, and more. This article provides an overview of the journey so far, its current state, and a glimpse into the promising technologies that will shape the future of cellular networks. It aims to serve as a concise reference for readers seeking a comprehensive understanding of the evolution of small cell networks from 4G to 6G. This article is expected to be a valuable resource for researchers and can be used as a teaching material for graduate and undergraduate students studying mobile communication and related disciplines. Additionally, it is anticipated that its content will be relevant for decades to come, serving as a mobile wireless expert's knowledge base. The authors anticipate that their work will contribute to advancing mobile communication technology and inspire future research in this field. This article is organized into 11 sections, starting with the introduction, followed by a historical review of cellular network evolution, and then discussing various technologies that will shape the future of mobile communication. Next, it highlights six emerging technologies that have the potential to revolutionize mobile communication, before summarizing the key takeaways from this article. Finally, the authors outline the main challenges and provide future directions for researchers in this field. The article concludes by emphasizing the importance of interdisciplinary collaboration to accelerate the development of 6G technology. The graph isomorphism problem's complexity varies greatly depending on the input graph, making it one of the most intriguing problems in computer science. A recent discovery by Devlin, Klavik, and Lozano demonstrates that if a finite graph G has its isomorphism problem solvable in polynomial time, then a subset of its vertices known as O(√|G|) can be identified, which enables isomorphism to be determined for any two graphs partially mapped together, based on the mapped subset. This leads to the concept of trimmed metric dimension, an extension of the metric dimension, where a subset of vertices, called the "pivot," allows determination of isomorphism for any two fully mapped graphs, based on their restriction to those vertices. It is shown that calculating the trimmed metric dimension requires at least √|G| space, proving a lower bound on the space complexity for the graph isomorphism problem. This finds applications in various fields including computer science, chemistry, and biology. Additionally, a linear-time algorithm is provided that can find a subset of vertices which allows isomorphism determination for any two fully mapped graphs, known as "2-strictly connected" subgraphs, and it is shown that such subgraphs can be found efficiently. Finally, it is shown that finding a subset which allows isomorphism determination for any two fully mapped graphs, known as "connected" subgraphs, requires exponential time and is likely to be NP-hard. This provides a lower bound on the complexity class of the graph isomorphism problem. This research provides a deeper understanding of the space complexity class and sheds light on the complexity of the graph isomorphism problem. It also opens up new avenues for research, providing efficient algorithms for finding certain subgraphs and shedding light on the hardness of finding others. It is also shown that the space complexity class of the graph isomorphism problem is not only influenced by the pivot's size but also by its structure. This research investigates an energy-efficient method to eliminate sulfur dioxide emissions, involving the sequential use of ozone and ultraviolet light. The rapid advancement of neuromorphic computing is driving innovation towards energy-efficient artificial intelligence systems that mimic the brain's processing mechanisms. To effectively develop and test these architectures, detailed design models are being developed using simulation tools such as SystemC. This modeling approach facilitates the simulation of electronic systems at a high abstraction level, enabling cycle-accurate modeling and the concurrent execution of design components. However, the existing SystemC-based models of neuromorphic computing architectures face challenges due to their complexity, limiting their ability to be shared across different platforms and making it difficult to test alternative compiler optimizations. To address these issues, a virtual platform has been developed to provide an open environment for designing and simulating neuromorphic computing systems. This platform features a modular design, allowing multiple neurons and synapses to be simulated concurrently, and includes support for common neuromorphic computing tasks. Furthermore, the virtual platform is compatible with popular simulation tools, such as Gem5 and QEMU, enabling the simulation of operating systems and application software on neuromorphic computing systems. The effectiveness of this approach has been demonstrated through the successful simulation of a 64-core neuromorphic computing system. The results show that the proposed virtual platform outperforms competing designs by up to 2.5 times in neural network inference tasks. Additionally, the platform allows for the exploration of novel compiler optimizations, yielding a 1.6 times improvement in latency and a 2 times improvement in energy efficiency in specific applications. The open-source code for this virtual platform has been made available online for the purpose of advancing neuromorphic computing research and development. However, there's a lack of research on how to effectively distribute testing-related feedback to students. Conventional approaches typically involve automated feedback mechanisms, but they often struggle to provide meaningful, actionable suggestions. In response, we've developed Inquiry-Based Testing Feedback (IBTF), a novel method that provides students with specific testing-related inquiries based on their test suite coverage. IBTF's primary goal is to improve students' code understanding by encouraging them to explore their code's intricacies while conducting tests. In this study, we compared the effects of IBTF and a more detailed human-provided feedback mechanism on the performance of undergraduate computer science students. Our results show that students receiving IBTF performed better and demonstrated improved code understanding, while also experiencing higher levels of engagement and satisfaction compared to those receiving traditional feedback. Notably, both groups exhibited similar improvement in their programming skills. Based on these findings, we believe IBTF offers an effective solution for distributing testing-related feedback, and we recommend its integration in existing testing tools to foster students' conceptual understanding. Additionally, IBTF's inquiry-based mechanism can be adapted to other educational tools, promoting students' critical thinking and problem-solving abilities through the distribution of clear, actionable feedback. In particular, we suggest examining its potential to improve students' critical thinking and problem-solving abilities. Furthermore, we believe that integrating IBTF into real-world software development projects could have a significant impact on the industry's overall quality. In the future, we plan to extend IBTF to cover other software engineering aspects, such as software documentation, to provide a more comprehensive learning experience for computer science students. By doing so, we believe IBTF can play a key role in promoting the distribution of conceptual feedback, ultimately enhancing the learning experience of software engineering students. Recent graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have achieved significant success in
various node-level prediction tasks, however, they demonstrate a common issue
known as over-blurring, meaning they struggle to learn precise model parameters
for individual nodes. Mathematically, over-blurring can be represented as the
average of neighbor node predictions, with the specific structure and mixing
ratio of these nodes immaterial. This unacceptably broad scope of GCN predictions
is the primary cause of over-blurring, with traditional approaches using multi-layer
perceptrons (MLPs) doing little to mitigate this issue. To tackle over-blurring,
we propose a novel, simple yet effective method called the Structured Graph Aware
GCN (SGAGCN), which incorporates an MLP that incorporates the local graph
structure into its design, thereby eliminating over-blurring and yielding
substantial performance improvements in various benchmark datasets. Furthermore,
we also establish a comprehensive benchmark to compare various current GCN
designs with our proposed SGAGCN. Extensive experimental results confirm the
substantial benefits of our proposed method in node-level prediction tasks. The
source code of our approach is available at https://github.com/zhengyu-1998/SGAGCN.

Research on remote epitaxy has gained significant interest due to its potential to grow single-crystalline layers on amorphous substrates, however the process's thorough comprehension is currently hindered by the lack of detailed studies. This paper delves into the epitaxial behavior of the L2M Heusler series with varying Mn content, when deposited on graphene coated sapphire, an amorphous substrate. By employing ab-initio calculations and scanning transmission electron microscopy, the research reveals that the remote epitaxy can transition into van der Waals epitaxy or pseudomorphic growth at increased deposition rates, this is attributed to the increased kinetic energy overcoming energetic barriers and allowing for bond relaxation. Furthermore, the study identifies the importance of initial island formation and the role of deposition rate in determining equilibrium layer heights. Ultimately, the findings provide valuable insights for optimizing remote epitaxy and achieving single-crystalline layers through this process. Moreover, the research suggests the potential for remote epitaxy to be rebranded as a form of van der Waals epitaxy or kinetic growth mode, and outlines avenues for further research to refine understanding of this phenomenon. Finally, the data also holds potential for advancing technological applications utilizing Heusler materials and more broadly, with implications for the optimization of various epitaxial growth techniques. This study provides evidence that bidders in auctions with a second-price payment method take their opponents' trustworthiness into account when making bidding decisions. Specifically, when initial interactions suggest an auction participant is untrustworthy, they tend to bid higher in future auctions, whereas those indicating they are trustworthy typically bid lower. Our results show that bidders who are considered untrustworthy tend to win auctions more frequently, likely due to their higher bidding tactics, despite also facing reduced participation from other bidders. To isolate the impact of trust dynamics, we employed an auction method where bidders can choose between two payments, their bid or a fixed amount chosen by the runner-up. Our findings indicate that trust dynamics in second-price auctions lead to qualitatively distinct bidding strategies, resulting in inferior outcomes for bidders relative to a scenario where trust is not a consideration. Moreover, these trust-related effects are resilient to changes in the auction environment, including adjustments to the number of bidders and the level of risk involved. Ultimately, we conclude that trust's influence on bidding behavior in second-price auctions is a significant factor, albeit one that is easily overlooked in theoretical analyses. We initiate a study of regular nilpotent Hessenberg varieties through a local coordinate system, deriving a geometric decomposition of their boundaries via a specialized vertex representation. This decomposition enabled us to demonstrate that the delta-set, a key concept in hyperplane arrangement theory, serves as the driving force behind the generation of Gr\"obner bases for the defining ideal of these varieties in a specific order. Furthermore, this analysis unlocks insights into the underlying singularities of the varieties, ultimately allowing us to reexamine and extend the classic Frobenius algebra and partition framework in light of this geometric decomposition. As a byproduct, our methods also yield an efficient algorithm for computing Gr\"obner bases for the defining ideal of Hessenberg varieties in a general setting, independent of Hessenberg shape. The underlying techniques employed are combinatorial and algebraic in nature, primarily utilizing the principles of Gr\"obner fans and limit posets. The proof of our findings also relies on established regular nilpotent Hessenberg variety properties, as well as the properties of certain finite poset arrangements. The presented work culminates in a comprehensive decomposition of regular nilpotent Hessenberg varieties, providing a potential foundation for future research in algebraic geometry, combinatorics, and the study of singularities. The accompanying appendices provide supplementary details, including a step-by-step algorithm for computing Gr\"obner bases and additional regular nilpotent Hessenberg variety examples. Acquiring knowledge through search engines like Google is essential to everyday life, yet little is known about how people form questions to seek answers. A study has been conducted to investigate this using a newly created dataset that includes a collection of individuals asked to pose questions about specific texts in exchange for monetary incentives. The research demonstrates that individuals tend to ask questions that cannot be easily resolved through a general search engine like Google, and those who frequently engage in online searches tend to formulate more effective Google-style queries. A dataset called ResearchQuests, which comprises 3,962 question-answer pairs, has been established and is accessible for free at https://researchquests.github.io. It comprises 1,502 questions from human subjects and 2,460 automatically generated queries based on a large corpus of research articles. The dataset also includes a comprehensive evaluation metric for assessing the suitability of questions for seeking answers through search engines. In addition, an analysis of neural network-based models for question generation reveals that they can benefit from additional training on this new dataset, and when combined with existing web data, their performance improves. The research also presents an innovative approach called Answer-Driven Question Filtering, which can automatically eliminate questions that cannot be answered through a search engine by analyzing its results. A comparison of this method with existing techniques reveals that it yields superior outcomes on multiple evaluation metrics. The research also introduces a new challenge, the Knowledge-Seeking Question Answering task, for the community to address, with more details available at https://ksqachallenge.github.io. This study investigates how a supernova model evolves in a specific environment, focusing on neutrino instabilities. Using a high-resolution 3D model, we examined neutrino properties and found that they exhibit significant variations within a small distance from the core. This phenomenon has the potential to impact the supernova's development, particularly by influencing its angular distribution. Additionally, we observed that neutrino instabilities are more prevalent near the supernova's boundary and are intensified by the interaction of neutrinos with the surrounding matter. This is in contrast to previous 1D models, which did not account for the complexities of supernova matter and instead assumed a uniform density. Our findings suggest that neutrino instabilities could play a crucial role in the supernova's development and provide valuable insights for future observations. This research also underscores the importance of accurately modeling three-dimensional supernova environments to gain a deeper understanding of core-collapse supernovae. Recent research has shown that machine learning can effectively identify Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) by analyzing resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) data, however the entire brain is not necessary to make this diagnosis. This study aimed to identify the essential brain regions for ADHD diagnosis by reducing rs-fMRI data while maintaining its original diagnostic capability. Using a novel deep learning approach that prioritizes data utility, the study constructed multiple rs-fMRI models with varying numbers of brain regions and corresponding reductions in data size. The outcome revealed that fully functional ADHD models can accurately diagnose the disorder with at least 68% accuracy when using the entire brain, but this capability declines with each additional restriction on the number of brain regions. When constrained to rs-fMRI data from 20 essential regions only, the models still exhibited high diagnostic accuracy for ADHD, with a 85% overall value. Notably, the study found that regions involving the default mode network, including the medial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate cortex, and temporal parietal regions, played a crucial role in ADHD diagnosis. The study's findings provide valuable insights into the underlying neural mechanisms of ADHD and can facilitate the development of more efficient and data-size-managed rs-fMRI models for ADHD diagnosis. In a discrete-time setting, we've developed an outbreak SISI model, where the binary states {0,1} represent susceptible and infectious individuals respectively, and the model is based on specific stochastic updates. By changing the time scale, we found that the model's non-trivial equilibrium occurs and can apply the Lasalle-Yorke theorem to show its stability. Moreover, we observed that the model exhibits chaotic behavior under certain conditions by calculating its largest Lyapunov exponent. This model can effectively simulate outbreaks in universities, as demonstrated using data from the COVID-19 pandemic at the University of Leicester. Our results reveal that the model's dynamics aligns well with real data, particularly in the initial stages of an outbreak, where the model's sensitivity to initial conditions plays a crucial role. Therefore, this model can serve as a valuable tool for preliminary outbreak predictions and planning purposes. All simulations were conducted using the programming language Python. Based on our research, we suggest that the model's parameters be adjusted according to an outbreak's severity level, with different sets of parameters leading to distinct dynamical behavior. Where an outbreak is mild, the model tends towards a stable equilibrium, whereas a severe outbreak results in chaotic dynamics. This approach enables us to simulate different scenarios, such as varying the number of susceptible and infectious individuals at different time scales. Furthermore, our research indicates that the model can effectively determine an outbreak's period and predict its trajectory up to 20 time steps in advance. While predicting an outbreak with high accuracy is challenging, our model can provide valuable insights for preliminary planning purposes. By changing the model's parameters, our research can effectively simulate outbreaks of different severity levels, making the model a versatile tool for various epidemiological applications. To analyze complex quantum systems, understanding the system's von Neumann entropy is crucial, yet measuring it directly is impractical due to its reliance on multiple copies of the state. We've developed two distinct protocols for approximating entropy in systems with limited dimensions, employing either single or few copies of the state. Our first protocol utilizes unitary design, resulting in an estimate with an $O(\sqrt{n})$ precision, while our second employs randomized methods, achieving an $O(n^{\frac{2}{3}})$ precision. Both protocols outperform prior non-quantum approaches, while also aligning with the established lower bound within an additive constant, thus providing a more accurate estimate than previous quantum methods. We've also adapted these protocols for constraint optimization problems derived from entropy, successfully solving the minimum output uncertainty problem with high precision even in high-dimensional systems. We've validated the performance of these algorithms through simulations based on random unitary design, while outlining potential future advancements in the field. Additionally, our work has led to the development of a new technique for generating designed unitary transformations with compact structure, which may have applications in quantum chemistry. Furthermore, our research has sparked an investigation into the influence of multiple measurement stages in random state estimation, revealing an optimal strategy that balances resources and accuracy, which could be applied beyond quantum settings as well. For effective clinical research and insurance claims analysis, accurate International Classification of Diseases (ICD) codes are crucial, but code quality is generally poor due to various errors in medical record systems. Currently, code correction relies on manual revision by clinical specialists, which is time-consuming and costly. Although deep learning techniques have shown promise in automating code correction, their application is limited by the need for a large, high-quality training dataset, which is rare for this task, even when supplemented with manual annotations. To address this challenge, this research proposes a semi-supervised learning framework that combines weakly labeled data from multiple sources and a small set of clinical specialists' manual revisions for code correction. The framework's ability to learn from imperfect data is enhanced by a custom-designed loss function that prioritizes specialist revisions and tolerates minor variations in raw data. The framework's efficiency and effectiveness were validated through extensive experiments using real-world data from a major healthcare institution, which yielded state-of-the-art performance in code correction. The developed method can now be applied to a broader range of medical code classification tasks. The well-documented Aldous-Broder and Wilson algorithms create random spanning trees with equal probability distributions, and since 1991, it has been known that running Wilson's algorithm for one excursion generates the same tree with probability 1. We will demonstrate that when Wilson's algorithm's tree construction process is halted after a single excursion, its resulting tree is also generated randomly with equal probability, thus establishing a temporary equivalence between the algorithms. Building on this equivalence and employing a two-stage approach, we will derive a general method to generate any n-vertex tree randomly and create a uniform spanning forest on n vertices with probability 1. Notably, our algorithm provides a straightforward, low-complexity solution for generating a uniform spanning tree, requiring only a single stage and involving constant additional memory storage beyond the tree's original storage capacity. Furthermore, we will show that our proposed method can be adapted to generate random oriented spanning trees with equal probability distributions in equal time. The article culminates by outlining potential future research directions related to our approach. This research introduces MusicTM-Dataset, a comprehensive set of data that enables cross-domain learning between sheet music, song lyrics, and musical audio. The dataset was created by combining three distinct sources: first, it collects sheet music from scores, along with accompanying lyrics, from various websites, resulting in a database of 1,500 unique song entries; second, it utilizes a pre-trained audio model to generate musical audio excerpts for each song, effectively establishing a link between the audio and sheet music; third, it leverages a pre-existing dataset of song lyrics to enhance its linguistic content. To validate the dataset's potential, it was used to train a basic cross-modal framework, which was then evaluated using a range of established metrics. Notably, the dataset's development facilitated several key insights: first, it was determined that cross-modal retrieval tasks can be effectively performed when guided by a relevant score-based representation; second, it was found that audio-generated excerpts can serve as a reasonable proxy for actual musical recordings; third, it was observed that sheet music and song lyrics exhibit distinct spatial distributions, yet musical audio and score representations exhibit a closer relationship. Ultimately, the MusicTM-Dataset is proposed as a valuable resource for fostering research in cross-modal learning, with a particular emphasis on addressing the challenges posed by sheet music, song lyrics, and musical audio. Additionally, the dataset and accompanying implementation details are openly available for public access at https://github.com/zhengyinli/MusicTM-Dataset. Although various concept hierarchies and networks have been explored, they often fail to consider how users interact with and navigate these concepts, which is essential for creating immersive learning experiences. To address this issue, we present Lotse, a flexible methodology and tool that helps domain experts create interactive knowledge structures tailored to users' needs. By leveraging Lotse, experts can define complex relationships between ideas and even link them to physical samples, all within a seamless workflow. Furthermore, Lotse enables seamless integration with popular visual analytics platforms, allowing users to access and navigate knowledge structures effortlessly. To demonstrate the effectiveness of Lotse, we showcase two real-world applications highlighting its practical value. We believe Lotse has the potential to revolutionize how domain expertise is shared and applied in visual analytics. To develop a systematic approach to promoting reaction speed, we examined the effects of gas flow rates, feed gas composition, and inlet temperature distributions on temperature arrangements in fixed beds.  Utilizing rapid magnetic resonance imaging to assess temperature variations, our research revealed that controlling gas dynamics rather than thermal conduction allows for precise manipulation of particle temperatures.  Additionally, our findings provide insight into the interplay between gas and particle temperature fluctuations, offering a basis for optimizing gas-solid contact and enhancing gas phase reaction kinetics.  This knowledge may also contribute to the development of efficient solid catalysts and also be applicable to other types of reactors, such as slurry reactors.  Future research will focus on extending the principles outlined in this study to promote uniform particle temperatures.

This paper examines a key application of the b-principle, a relatively new concept in geometric methods that emphasize flexibility and abstraction. The b-principle can be seen as a flexible metaphor for flexible mathematical structures, and it finds its highest level of abstraction in the form of the homotopy b-principle, a powerful tool that has been instrumental in solving multiple high-profile mathematical problems over the course of the 21st century. One of the most notable problems that the b-principle has helped to resolve is the celebrated Nash problem, a challenge that had gone unsolved for nearly six decades before being conquered through the combined efforts of multiple mathematicians. This paper represents a specific instance in which the b-principle is applied to address a complex problem, namely the combination of the Freedman conjecture and the Morin conjecture, which concern the topology of certain critical point configurations in manifold geometry known as singularities. The analysis relies on an extension of the b-principle known as the local version, a refinement that takes into account the local topological characteristics of the target space manifold. This refined approach, combined with additional geometric constructions, ultimately yields a complete proof of both conjectures, a result that had been previously verified through other methods only as recently as 2008 for the Freedman conjecture and in 2018 for the Morin conjecture. This research presents the development of an electro-mechanical heart model using advanced finite element methods. Due to the large size of the heart and its interconnected tissues, the mathematical problem is inherently multi-scale and poses significant computational challenges. To overcome these obstacles, the study focuses on designing an efficient iterative solution method combining advanced techniques such as multigrid algorithms, sparse matrix splitting, and adaptive finite element methods. Through thorough examinations of various system properties, such as non-zero pattern inheritance and boundary condition enforcement, the study introduces a novel multilevel preconditioner. Subsequent benchmark tests using standard heart models reveal substantial speedups in computation, with up to 25 times faster solution times for large problem sizes. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that its multilevel preconditioner outperforms existing alternatives in cardiac simulations, particularly when coupling electrical and mechanical forces into a unified system. To facilitate widespread adoption, the study makes available open-source software for replicating the research findings. Ultimately, the findings contribute to the advancement of simulation-based clinical trials in cardiology by providing guidance on implementing efficient numerical methods. Given the diverse applications of the ALBERTA model, spanning cardiology, neurology, and dentistry, the research is expected to have far-reaching implications for computational biology and medicine. Recently, proposed acoustic metagratings utilize transformed gratings to manipulate sound waves across a broad frequency range, exceeding human hearing. Although optical research has demonstrated the potential of these structures, their technical application in ultrasonic frequencies is yet to be realized. This study presents an innovative approach to develop acoustic metagratings operating at frequencies above 100 kHz, where traditional manufacturing methods are impractical. By leveraging two-photon polymerization, we crafted complex microstructures with intricate geometries that effectively refract sound waves. Experimental results show promising results, matching simulations with notable gains in sound wave transmission and unique acoustic properties. These advancements pave the way for novel devices, such as sound lenses and manipulators. Additionally, integrating these structures with microelectromechanical systems may enable novel applications in sensing, communication, and other areas. This knowledge could also translate to the manipulation of other waves, expanding our understanding of wave physics. This research has been documented in a recent issue of Nature Communications, where more details can be found (Kusuma et al., Nature Communications volume 10, number 1, 2022). Please refer to the original paper for further information. Implementing industrial automation systems in mines poses a difficult task due to frequent equipment and network disruptions. Mobile Internet of Audiovisual Things (IABT) has been proposed as a solution, allowing the creation of robust and reliable automation systems despite these obstacles. However, integrating mobile IABT in industrial applications is hindered by several challenges which need to be addressed by the technical community. This study aims to highlight these difficulties and suggest possible approaches to tackle them, with the ultimate goal of promoting mobile IABT in industrial settings. To this end, we outline specific scenarios where mobile IABT can be applied to solve practical problems and increase the efficiency of industrial processes. Furthermore, we highlight key research issues and potential solutions to these problems, and finally, outline the relevant standards that need to be developed or refined to support mobile IABT in industry. By contributing to this discussion, we hope to pave the path for mobile IABT applications in industry. Keywords: Industrial Automation, Mobile Internet of Audiovisual Things, IoAT, Industrial Networks, Audiovisual Assistants.

When conducting global sensitivity analysis, the focus is on assessing how various inputs, such as hyperparameters, influence the outcomes of more intricate models, like evolutionary algorithms. By employing a multi-faceted approach combining statistical and machine learning techniques, along with a Bayesian framework, we can gain a deeper understanding of these sensitivity relationships. Building on previous research, our study expands the scope to 20 different hyperparameters from seven EVAlgorithm types, utilizing a dataset containing 1,520 experimentations. The results from our global sensitivity analysis indicate that some evolutionary algorithms are more resilient to variations in their hyperparameters than others, with the effectiveness of these hyperparameters also being examined. To facilitate further research, our methodology is made available as an open-source tool. Furthermore, our study highlights the importance of properly tuning hyperparameters for open-source evolutionary algorithms to enhance their overall performance. Additionally, our research suggests that an optimal hyperparameter configuration can significantly boost an evolutionary algorithm's ranking in comparative evaluations. Lastly, our findings also shed light on the minimum number of runs required to draw reliable conclusions based on the results of these experiments. To summarize, our research aims to contribute to the ongoing quest for more robust and efficient evolutionary algorithms through global sensitivity analysis. This paper seeks to address this gap by establishing its justification through operator-theoretic methods. Additionally, this paper also explores the wave formula's counterpart in relativistic systems, which involves the Dirac equation, but does not provide its justification. Nonetheless, similar reasoning is provided to justify the relativistic version of the wave formula. This research paper draws inspiration from earlier works by Kato, Simon, and Tang-Erdoğan, which examined various differential equations in an analogous context. One notable difference in this current study is that it derives solutions for a non-normal operator, in contrast to its classical counterpart, which requires the operator to be normal. Consequently, this research employs non-normal perturbation theory and other distinct techniques, resulting in a unique approach. Reinforcement learning has achieved significant success in various areas, but numerous obstacles remain for its widespread application in real-world settings, particularly when transferring skills across domains. To evaluate lifelong reinforcement learning methods and identify their strengths and weaknesses, we introduce an open-source platform called L2Explorer. This environment presents a comprehensive setup that enables lifelong reinforcement learning research through multiple interconnected domains, designed to mimic a video game scenario where skills are acquired to access new levels and objectives. Our framework includes a client-server architecture, allowing for flexible research designs and streamlining the evaluation process. L2Explorer is designed to be adaptable for various research objectives and provides implementable code to support replication of the experimental results presented in the research paper. The platform will be accessible at https://l2explorer.com/. Further details on the code can be found at https://github.com/learning2learn/l2explorer.

We experimentally investigate the optical properties of coupled biomolecular complexes that contain chlorophyll, connected to a linear optical system, and demonstrate the manipulation of their polarization using light of varying colors. Our results reveal a method to control the polarization of emitted light without its interaction with electrical currents, and show that localized changes in one component of the complex can affect others even when they are not physically connected. Additionally, we observed a unique phenomenon where the polarization of connected complexes changes in response to changes in their internal light interactions. These findings have the potential to improve the performance of optical photovoltaic devices and enable new technologies for controlling light with biological materials. Finally, we connect our research to a potential biological process known as photosynthesis.

This research paper focuses on the COVID-19 pandemic's impact on South Africa, highlighting the country's response through data-driven decision making. By aggregating this information, we created an accessible data repository facilitating COVID-19 analysis and modeling through the application of statistical and machine learning techniques. Our research showcases its methodology and achievements, emphasizing the importance of open-access data in informing policy during the pandemic. It also lays the groundwork for future non-COVID related studies, as well as potential extensions to our approach, such as incorporating missing data through machine learning algorithms. Our findings are grounded on an empirical case study conducted in the Western Cape province, where we employed open-access data to model the pandemic's progression and evaluate non-pharmaceutical interventions. Our model successfully replicated the province's pandemic trajectory with satisfactory accuracy, enabling policymakers to simulate the impact of different measures on the outbreak. Our research demonstrates that integrating accessible data can mitigate the country's pandemic response challenges, while also creating opportunities for data-driven research and development. An additive number system's initial term counts the sum of four distinct elements, and subsequent terms are generated by iteratively taking sums of combinations of previous terms, where combinations can't repeat any values. Freiman's 3k-4 theorem reveals that if a set with roughly four times as many elements satisfies this definition, it must significantly overlap with the sum of four sets with roughly equal populations. We present an expanded version of Freiman's theorem, applying it to number systems that use different operations besides addition. Additionally, our analysis provides support for Connes' embedding conjecture, particularly in its "local" form known as the "noncommutative Freiman problem." Our proof also strengthens a prior result by Bergelson, Hindman, and Alford, which had imposed a 12k+1 requirement for overlapping sets. We anticipate that our 9k+1 requirement is also replaceable with a more flexible condition. Lastly, we speculate that our 9k+1 requirement could even be reduced to a condition directly related to the size of k. Finally, we utilize two distinct approaches to demonstrate that our analysis is, in fact, precise up to a factor of 25 with respect to the size of k. One approach relies on the analysis of a specific category of infinite groups known as "freiman groups," while the other involves the manipulation of a complex mathematical structure known as a "category of finite freiman groups." We also introduce a novel concept, "freiman sets," by which we derive upper limits for the size of groups that fit within a particular framework known as the freiman theorem. We then utilize the strategy of "forcing," a method initially developed by mathematicians Albert and Reinhart, to demonstrate that our analysis is, in fact, precise up to a factor of 25 with respect to the size of k. We also explore the limits of our analysis through the examination of "freiman sets" with specific structural properties known as "abelian" and "nonabelian" properties. We also present an expanded version of Freiman's theorem that applies to number systems with up to three distinct elements in each term, revealing a significant overlap between a set and the sum of three sets with roughly equal populations, provided that it satisfies certain conditions. In response to the COVID-19 pandemic, hospitals have implemented strict capacity controls, leading to critical shortages of intensive care unit beds, which necessitate early and accurate prediction of high-risk patients for timely allocation of resources. To address this need, we propose identifying key characteristics of ICU admissions from chest X-ray images, which can help predict patients in need of ICU care and aid in prioritizing bed allocation during the pandemic. We began by collecting a dataset of 14,245 X-ray images from MIMIC-CT and COVID-19-RX, but due to data inconsistencies, we selected 9,563 images for our study after data preprocessing. We utilized a VGG-16 model and modified it by adding PSPMax, ReLU, and Softmax layers to extract features from the images. We then utilized nine potential attributes to construct our model and evaluated its performance using AUC-ROC and F1-score metrics. Our results showed that our model accurately predicted eight attributes with high precision and accurately predicted the remaining attribute with moderate precision. Additionally, our study found that our model effectively predicted patients in need of ICU care and compared favorably to existing models, while also highlighting the potential benefits and limitations of our approach for clinical use. We will make our preprocessed data and VPP-VGG16 model publicly available to facilitate further research on this topic. We will also conduct further research to expand our dataset and improve our model by incorporating more attributes and more advanced deep learning models. We aim to make our findings more actionable by incorporating InceptionV3 and incorporating decision rules to identify specific image features that contribute to our model's predictions. We hope that our research will contribute to the development of a system that utilizes chest X-ray images to accurately predict patients in need of ICU care and aids in bed allocation during the pandemic and in general clinical practice. We will make our data and model publicly available at https://github.com/ahmed-omar/Potential-Attributes-of-ICU-admission-in-X-ray-images-of-COVID-19-patients. We will also present our research at the 2022 IEEE 20th International Conference on Information Intelligence and Integration, which will be held at the University of Texas at Dallas from November 28 to December 1, 2022. This research addresses the problem of recovering a piecewise-constant radial function representing boundary conditions for the Helmholtz equation in dimensions one and two, using analytically derived transmission eigenfunctions with distinct frequencies as input. By leveraging the unique phase information inherent to transmission eigenfunctions, this study develops a theoretical framework for constructing the radial function through a Fourier space transformation, thereby extending existing surface scattering protocols to enable boundary identification. Utilizing perfectly conducting and acoustic media as examples, our numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed method can effectively recover boundary conditions at various scales using synthesis and phase unwrapping analysis. Additionally, this study showcases its capability to handle irregularly scaled phases by implementing a modified approach. Valuable insights into medium properties can also be obtained from the Fourier transform magnitude, highlighting the potential for feature extraction and imaging purposes. Overall, this research provides a novel and efficient method for boundary identification using transmission eigenfunctions. Due to their theoretical derivation, these eigenfunctions can be calculated even in cases where scattering data may be unavailable, thereby enabling medium boundary recovery even in such scenarios. Furthermore, this study's phase-based approach offers advantages in noise reduction over traditional back-propagation surface reconstruction techniques. Finally, the proposed method facilitates quantitative analysis and estimation of material parameters, thereby supporting a wide range of applications in geophysics and geology that rely on surface or airborne data. These parameters include skin thickness, ice layer properties, and buried object depth, among others. By extending phase information to these applications, this study opens up new avenues for research in computational geophysics. At the theoretical level, this research confirms that transmission eigenfunctions can effectively capture boundary conditions, thereby supporting their use in various inverse scattering problems and related inquiries. Furthermore, the proposed method has the potential to be adapted for other inverse problems and imaging applications, potentially enabling novel and efficient computational methods for data acquisition and processing. Finally, this study demonstrates that transmission eigenfunctions can be utilized as a data representation that is scale- and medium-dependent, thereby offering a new perspective on scattering data and its potential for parameter estimation and imaging purposes. These findings are expected to contribute significantly to the development of innovative algorithms and methods in computational geophysics and related fields. To expand a dialogue system's capabilities and adapt to unforeseen user intentions, we propose a novel approach called NID. NID identifies new user objectives through observed conversation effects and corrects any interpretation discrepancies. Our two-stage NID methodology comprises self-driving learning of user intents facilitated by a pre-trained language model and a adaptive training technique based on contrastive learning. The initial stage utilizes a pre-trained model to gather data and involves two processes: intent classification and intent source prediction. The second stage refines the model's performance using a dynamic sampling method that contrasts positive with negative samples. Our approach enhances a dialogue system's responsiveness, achieving success rates 20-30% higher than the current standard method, namely iterative user feedback, across three evaluation benchmarks. Moreover, our NID approach exhibits scalability benefits in both data collection and adaptation for new user intentions. Our research demonstrates that NID accelerates a dialogue system's development while maintaining similar safety standards as user feedback-based methods. We demonstrate that the universal simplicial collection defined by Bénabou and M\'eliotto in relation to simplicial categories, is in fact a simplicial group under a specific operation that adheres to the principles of associativity, unity, and invertibility. This finding expands on prior research by Grandis and Stramaccia, who proved the simplicial nature of the universal simplicial group defined by Bénabou. Furthermore, we establish that the homotopy theory of the developed collection category is equivalent to that of the collection category of the original simplicial categories. Additionally, we present a method to compute the collection homotopy type of any abstract simplicial group, accompanied by an algorithm to determine if a collection homotopy type corresponds to a group homotopy type. Lastly, we present an analysis of the collection homotopy types that can be realized as group homotopy types, along with a specific criterion for achieving this equivalence, which in turn enables the identification of the collection homotopy types that are also group homotopy types that are also simplicial groups in the classical sense. This research culminates in the discovery that a collection homotopy type corresponds to a group homotopy type if and only if its collection face functors exhibit a specific form of strict monic coherence. This finding holds significant implications for the study of higher order invariants in homotopy theory. Furthermore, we present an explicit example of a collection homotopy type that does not correspond to a group homotopy type, along with a proposed open problem related to homotopy theory. Lastly, we present a method to compute the collection homotopy type of any abstract simplicial group defined by Bénabou. In our analysis, we demonstrate that a finite group of order $r$ has no more than $$7.3972\cdot\exp\left(\frac{\log r}{4}\right)$$ subgroups. This estimate is precise enough to show that there is no finite group with exactly 79 subgroups. Previously, the maximum number of subgroups in a finite group of order $r$ had an upper limit of $$\exp\left(\frac{\log r}{4}+\frac{\log\log r}{3}+\frac{\log p}{2}\right)$$ where $p$ is the smallest prime divisor of $r$. Our research builds upon work by McLaughlin and Tiep, and uses recent findings by the second author in character degree calculations. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the established limits are close to the actual values, as evidenced by our investigation of the number of subgroups in simple groups. Finally, our research poses several questions for further exploration. \\ \\ \textbf{Note:} Upon submitting this paper, we became aware of a related result by Giudici, Guralnick, and Marócz in arXiv:2103.14311, where they show that there is no finite group with exactly 79 subgroups. Our research, however, provides a more general upper limit for the number of subgroups in a finite group. \\ \\ \textbf{Note:} Upon submitting this paper, we became aware of a related result by Giudici, Guralnick, and Marócz in arXiv:2103.14311, where they show that there is no finite group with exactly 79 subgroups. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed loss function through experimental validation on the V-COCO dataset. Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have led to a surge in research at the intersection of quantum computing and deep neural networks, known as quantum deep learning. To address the inherent issues of current deep neural networks in handling loss, propagation, and dimensionality, researchers are incorporating quantum mechanics into neural networks. This article delves into various quantum neural network architectures that have been proposed, highlighting their benefits and drawbacks. Furthermore, it explores two areas where quantum neural networks have been successfully applied: solving complex optimization problems and mimicking intricate probability distributions. In addition, the challenges posed by existing quantum neural networks and potential avenues for resolution are discussed, including resolving query complexity, addressing no-zero error issues, and mitigating the negative impact of noise during execution. It's hypothesized that combining classical and quantum elements, a practice known as hybrid computing, could be key to overcoming these hurdles. Ultimately, the article concludes with a discussion of the future prospects of quantum neural networks and their potential to revolutionize various fields with quantum deep learning. We have derived and analyzed the low-frequency and long-wavelength properties of wave propagation within a relativistic system of fluids non-viscous and viscous nature. The results reveal harmonically oscillating relationships across the spectrum, regardless of the presence of viscosity. Comparison with existing theories and models in non-viscous and viscous systems has been conducted. Additionally, we have demonstrated that our derived equations align with first-order approximations in both non-viscous relativistic hydrodynamics and first-order relativistic hydrodynamics. Furthermore, we have explored the implications of our findings on boundary conditions at surfaces and the recovery of the non-viscous relativistic hydrodynamics limit. Lastly, we have examined if the derived equations can be applied to quark-gluon plasma by considering the values of specific parameters. Although the coefficients may vary greatly due to the strong interaction, the universal behavior of harmonically oscillating relationships across the spectrum is expected to hold within the relevant temperature range of quark-gluon plasma. With this information, we have simulated and plotted the relationships for non-viscous and viscous cases in quark-gluon plasma. Furthermore, we have derived similar relationships for conformal quark plasma with the assistance of hard thermal loops. The results reveal similar patterns in both systems, with the exception of a divergence in certain parameters at quark-gluon plasma due to the strong interaction. The analysis also sheds light on the feasibility of deriving similar relationships for other systems, such as nuclear matter and neutron stars, by taking into account the finite density of these systems. The resulting relationships across various states of matter are expected to share similar characteristics. This research introduces the Virtual Safeguard Platform, a novel, five-stage pipelined VHDL CPU design built on the Topaz Framework for High-Efficiency (TFHE), which is based on the Brakerski-Gilboa-Villard (BGV) scheme. The study demonstrates that the VSP architecture can efficiently support encryption-breaking attacks while the TFHE-based system remains securely protected. To validate the efficacy of the VSP model, performance testing was carried out using the SPECint2000 benchmark suite under different key sizes, yielding a five-stage pipelined VSP with 256-bit and 768-bit encryption keys, respectively. Furthermore, the analysis shows that increasing the key size enhances the system's security against side-channel attacks without a noticeable performance decline. Moreover, the research found that the side-channel resistance offered by the VSP model surpasses that of similar systems based on the CKKS scheme. Finally, the findings emphasize that the VSP architecture can effectively safeguard sensitive data within embedded systems from malicious users while maintaining robust protection against advanced side-channel attacks. This research is expected to contribute to the development of protected software solutions. The VSP source code is available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/AbdullahAlnafie/VSP.git. We have derived a polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) for a broad class of optimization problems that yield vector-valued outputs even when some constraints have limited opacity. Our approach leverages a recent PTAS for a similar vector-valued problem, and our results also extend to more restrictive single-source sparse data flow analysis by achieving better approximation than previous methods, albeit with a higher approximation rate. Our experiments with applying these algorithms to four real-world problems - code analysis, device mapping, tile mapping, and phase retrieval - demonstrate substantial reductions in solution size with minimal impact on accuracy. These findings suggest that, in practice, the focus on finding exact solutions may be unnecessary, and overemphasizing accuracy could lead to overly large solution sizes. The rapid rotation of young stars at the surface, also known as "spinning up," can be explained by various theories, but the specific mechanism responsible remains unknown. Researchers have found that the rotation of stars in the Upper Main Sequence (UMS) stage varies greatly and can be better explained by models that include turbulent internal movement than those relying solely on viscosity, suggesting that these stars may have undergone significant internal changes since forming.
