Building on Savitch's work in the 1970s, which showed in the context of Turing machines that multiplication can be achieved in linear time if addition takes constant time, our research expands upon this by determining under which conditions for any given arithmetic operation $op$, if it can be performed at $t(n)$ time on a single input of size $n$, it can also be carried out in roughly the same time $t(n)$ on two inputs of sizes $n_1$ and $n_2$ respectively, even if they are stored in separate locations of the memory. Our results reveal that operations like division, modulo, exponentiation, and root-taking can be performed at a constant rate of time if and only if multiplication can be. Additionally, we establish the converse - that if an operation can be performed at a constant rate of time, so can its variants with reduced precision, provided the loss of precision does not exceed a certain threshold without a proportionate reduction in input size. Furthermore, we show that basic arithmetic operations like multiplication, division, and root-finding can be performed at a constant rate of time if and only if they can be achieved using only addition, subtraction, and comparison operations. Our research also yields an unexpected finding that previously known results by Borodin, Munro, and Rall in the context of read-only Turing machines, which showed that multiplication, division, and root-finding can be performed at a constant rate of time if and only if addition can, is actually valid under a broader set of conditions. Lastly, we resolve an open problem from a 2019 workshop on the fundamental limits of the RAM model by proving that if multiplication can be performed at a constant rate of time, so can the computation of the minimum and maximum values in an array. Our research employs novel techniques that combine ideas from non-deterministic computation and the study of circuits. We introduce an innovative technique called photo-induced transient voltage (PITVE) for analyzing three-dimensional charge transport in diamond. By emitting two photons with different polarizations, we can distinguish free charge and trapped-dipole activation, while a spatial map of the diamond's charge transport properties is obtained through measurement of the temporal variation in the refractive index. When tested on a 3.4 mm thick type IIa diamond, we observed two-stage transport dynamics, with the sub-diamond region exhibiting significantly faster charge transfer compared to its edges. Furthermore, we successfully demonstrated the capability to resolve spatial variations within a 1 mm x 1 mm area on the diamond's surface. This technique offers a unique means of studying charge transport in diamond and holds significant potential for applications in photonic devices. PITVE's primary benefits include non-invasive measurement and the ability to analyze diamond samples at room temperature following exposure to two-photon absorption. Following the introduction of this approach, we anticipate its widespread adoption in the research community for analyzing diamond charge transport properties. Due to its versatility, this technique can also be applied to other semiconductors beyond diamond. With further refinement, we expect PITVE to facilitate the design and development of innovative diamond-based photonic devices. Given its potential to capture spatial information, we envision its application in measuring the spatially-resolved temporal variation in the diamond's charge transport properties. This could significantly contribute to advancements in diamond technology by enabling precise measurement of its charge transport characteristics. By combining PITVE with existing techniques, we may uncover novel insights into the underlying physics of charge transport in diamond, potentially leading to breakthroughs in its applications as a semiconductor and in diamond-based photonic device design. Soft grippers are increasingly popular in robotics due to their low cost, flexibility, and ability to adapt. However, their deformation under load makes it challenging for control algorithms to function effectively, even though simulation models are typically available. This paper presents a novel online algorithm that integrates dynamic simulation models and control strategies via the Koopman operator framework. The algorithm addresses issues such as variable initial conditions, external disturbances, and model inaccuracies in soft grippers, which can be modeled as switched linear differential equations. The method first generates an effective model for discrete time evolution using Koopman operator theory and then applies it to design a linear quadratic predictive control. The algorithm iteratively refines its control estimates and system state predictions in real-time. Experimental results on a multi-fingered soft gripper demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in tracking desired trajectories and maintaining grip stability. The study highlights the potential for Koopman operator theory to bridge the gap between simulated and real-world behavior in soft robotics applications. A video showcasing the algorithm's performance is available at https://youtu.be/6Q6Q8xkY7Gw. The research was financially supported by the National Science Foundation's grant number 1734547. The simulation and hardware environment used in the study can be accessed via https://github.com/roboticslab-ucbv/SoftGripper and https://github.com/roboticslab-ucbv/KoopmanSDC, respectively. One of the most fundamental and widely employed optimization techniques in deep
learning is the stochastic gradient descent (SGD), yet it has a major limitation
because its parameters are tightly coupled, making it difficult to generalize and
apply to multiple models efficiently. This led to the development of the organic
gradient descent (OGD), a method that can handle multiple parameters in an
unstructured manner and maintain generalized parameters for all models. This paper
demonstrates the effectiveness of OGD by showing its capabilities in applying the
learned parameters across various architectures and also achieving faster convergence
when compared to traditional SGD with adaptive learning rate methods like Adam. Even
though OGD has a higher time complexity than SGD, its performance in parameter
re-use makes it a viable option for large-scale deep learning applications, and hence
this paper also presents an efficient OGD variant with reduced time and space
complexity, dubbed VOGD, which strikes a balance between performance and
efficiency. The empirical results and source code are available for reproducibility.

We conducted detailed studies of a hyperactive quasar, J2102+6015, at a distance of approximately 18.7 billion light-years from Earth. Our observations revealed a complex pattern consisting of a compact core and three distinct lobes aligned in an east-west direction. We measured the size of this structure at approximately 38 kHz frequency, determining it to be around 190 kiloparsecs in diameter. Additionally, our data indicated that the energy released over the lifetime of this quasar exceeded the energy stored. Based on this information, we assigned J2102+6015 the classification of an FR II quasar during its mature phase. Notably, its spectral ages are significantly younger than its observed lifetime, which could be attributed to significant lobe growth during its early stages or multiple active phases. We also utilized archival data at higher frequencies to determine the source's morphology and compare it to existing images, revealing significant evolution in its structure over time. Our findings indicate that J2102+6015 exhibits characteristics of both an FR I and FR II quasar, depending on the observation frequency and epoch. We also present multiwavelength photometry of the quasar, including its broad band magnitudes, spectral indices, and colors. Lastly, we added J2102+6015 to the Faint Quasar Survey, a comprehensive catalog of faint quasars observed using the Very Large Array. This inclusion brings the total number of quasars in this catalog to 342.

This research delves into the relationship between Lung Cancer Phenotypes and Patient Lifespan, utilizing data from The Cancer Imaging Archive. By combining imaging data with clinical information, our findings reveal that Lymph Node Metastases play a crucial role in determining patient outcomes. Building on this discovery, we develop a Multimodal Prognostic System, integrating Radiological and Pathological data, which outperforms models relying solely on imaging information. We further investigate the effectiveness of Phenotype-based Models and Models trained on individual Tumor Regions. Our study demonstrates that Lung Cancer Phenotypes are strongly linked to Patient Outcomes and that Radiological and Pathological data complement each other in predicting patient prognosis. Additionally, our results indicate that analyzing specific Tumor Regions can contribute to accurate prognosis. With high accuracy, our system can identify patients at risk of dying within five years following diagnosis, paving the way for the development of personalized treatment and medication plans. Due to the rapid dissemination of information on social media, it's crucial to constantly analyze
public sentiment. This study seeks to demonstrate the effectiveness of using Long Short-Term
Memory (LSTM) networks, a type of recurrent neural network, in assessing Twitter user sentiment.
We created two binary classification models, one using real-world data from the Kaggle dataset and
another utilizing our custom dataset, both focusing on categorizing tweets as either positive or
negative. We also explored the impact of preprocessing our data by converting all words to lower
case and removing stop words, which led to improved model accuracy in our experiments. The results
show that using an LSTM framework resulted in higher accuracy rates compared to a basic recurrent
neural network. With an accuracy rate of 87.35% on our dataset and 92% on the Kaggle dataset,
our research indicates that LSTM networks can effectively classify Twitter user sentiment. Given
the growing importance of sentiment analysis, this study contributes to the ongoing discussion on
using deep learning techniques for social media sentiment analysis. With deep neural networks like
LSTM continuously outperforming other methods in this area, they are poised to revolutionize the
field of social media sentiment analysis. Additionally, incorporating data preprocessing into our
methods enhances our accuracy, underscoring the importance of combining cutting-edge neural
networks with fundamental data science techniques to achieve optimal results in Twitter sentiment
analysis. The Python code for this project has been made publicly available on GitHub at

To effectively engage users, a conversational system must adhere to its designated role. Traditionally, natural language processing approaches have focused on either user or system-initiated dialogue, despite role-based conversation being common in both cases. Prior work on role-based conversation involves either ignoring the constraint or attempting to enforce it through post-processing, which can lead to awkward responses. This paper proposes a novel method that utilizes a parameter-optimized open-domain dialogue model and a role-specified residual network to ensure natural conversations that conform to the assigned role. Our approach was evaluated using human evaluators, who found our system's responses to be both relevant and role-appropriate in 87% of cases, with the remaining 13% being minor deviations. Additionally, our study indicates that this model prioritizes role adherence at the expense of overall conversation quality by a margin of 0.05 in subjective evaluation. Our dialogue system was successfully demonstrated to a group of participants, who were able to engage in 5-minute conversations that met the role standard in 80% of cases, with the remaining 20% showing minor lapses. Notably, this model outperformed non-role-based models in both role-relatedness and conversation effectiveness, according to the participants' assessments. Our findings indicate that role-based conversation can be effectively utilized in open-domain dialogue systems, even when the role is specified, which may have implications for future research in this field. Our code and dataset are available for download at https://github.com/ChenYiYun2020/Role-Constrained-Open-Domain-Dialogue. Our system is also accessible via a user-friendly interface at https://www.ailab.srhu.edu.cn/RoleConstrainedOpenDomainDialogue/. It provides users with a platform to interact with our role-based open-domain dialogue system, which can be utilized in both user- and system-initiated conversations. Users can specify their desired role in the conversation, which will be enforced by the system to ensure natural and role-compliant interactions. Our system aims to serve as a versatile tool for research in role-based conversation and may be adapted for various applications in natural language processing. With its ability to effectively engage users in conversations that meet specified role criteria, this system holds significant potential for enhancing the interaction between humans and computers. Moreover, our findings may contribute to advancements in open-domain dialogue systems, which can be optimized for role-relatedness at the expense of overall conversation quality. Our research has significant implications for natural language processing and may pave the way for more innovative applications of role-based conversation

This background might be identifiable if future detectors at new wavelengths are able to detect a significant number of sources per day, especially if they are able to distinguish the scattered signal from the initial burst emitted by these collisions. Additionally, we determined that the scattered background could provide valuable information about the population dynamics and spatial distribution of compact object formations in the local universe. However, the scattered signal is unlikely to be the primary contributor to the overall gravitational wave background in the mHz frequency range that LISA is designed to detect. Furthermore, our model predicts the generation of dark matter, with a density roughly 10% that of ordinary matter, as a result of neutrino oscillations. The same hidden sector that gives rise to dark matter and gravitational waves also enables the spontaneous generation of a baryon excess. Specifically, we've considered two scenarios: one involving a relatively slow phase transition and another with an extremely rapid transition. In the slow case, the gravitational waves' amplitude will be significant at around 10^-17, while the rapid transition will yield much weaker signals, approximately 10^-20 in amplitude. A key objective of artificial intelligence is to create robots that can effectively interact with others, assuming a certain level of mutual understanding exists. However, if no common framework exists for communication, robots may not be able to achieve this goal. We propose the "signaling game" as a means to establish a common language for interaction, allowing robots to create a shared understanding through observation and learning. We demonstrate the integration of the signaling game with an information-theoretic approach called "semantic mashup," which enables robots to emerge and use a common language to exchange information. We showcase our method in a complex causal reasoning task, where robots learn to observe and predict the effects of moving objects through either verbal or non-verbal cues. The emerged language plays a crucial role in the robots' ability to solve problems, such as identifying the object's cause-and-effect relationship based on observed visual and auditory signals. We provide detailed analysis and findings from experiments conducted in simulated and real environments, highlighting the significance of our approach in grounded semantic learning. Unlike existing methods that either assume a pre-existing common language or restrict interactions to a single modality, our approach offers a more realistic and versatile means for emergent semantic exchanges between robots. With this method, robots can learn to effectively communicate through multiple modalities and achieve a shared understanding of complex causal events simply by observing and predicting the effects of moving objects. This approach aims to mitigate the underfitting often associated with Naive Bayes on complex datasets.  • An innovative strategy for generating negative samples by incorporating latent features, which enables a pre-trained classifier to identify potential terms without access to their actual features. This technique aims to enhance the classifier's ability to recognize terms with obscure or hidden characteristics.  • An adaptive sampling method that adjusts its focus based on the current prediction phase, either maximizing recall by sampling randomly or optimizing precision by selecting closely related terms, all while operating within a specified time constraint. Experimental evaluations on two benchmark datasets, along with detailed analysis, demonstrate that Hybrid Model 3.0 outperforms existing solutions in terms of recall, precision, F1-score, and micro-F1-score. Recent advances in session-based recommendation have shown great potential in
addressing the needs of users who interact with products on an episodic basis.
However, existing session-based methods primarily focus on single session
predictions, overlooking long-term behavioral patterns that are critical for
long-term sustainability. To address this gap, we introduce an approach that
leverages session data and encodes historical information into implicit
long-term preferences. Our framework comprises two modules: one that recommends
products within a single session and another that aggregates preferences across
multiple sessions. To enhance single-session recommendations, we employ Rank
Embeddings, allowing the model to learn synergistic interactions among candidate
items. We further develop Candidate Rank Embeddings to capture item properties
and their enduring impact on user behavior. Experimental results on four large
datasets demonstrate that our proposed method surpasses several baseline
recommendation algorithms, with notable improvements quantified as 3.0%,
4.1%, 2.0%, and 2.3% gains in terms of metric MRR, evaluated across MAMER,
ML-20M-Users, TAO, and AmazonCoBuy-Dataset-2G. Our approach's superiority is
further validated by community developers, showcasing the potential for

Wikipedia's extensive knowledge base is powered by a vast community of editors, whose work ranges from creating engaging articles to fighting vandalism, resulting in a significant amount of low-grade, unverified content along the way, which is beneficial but lacks labels for reference purposes, posing a problem for their utilization. This research aims to address this challenge by developing an automated method to annotate these articles, focusing on how editing behaviors correlate with content quality. Through computational analysis, our model identified three distinct categories of editors, characterized by their contributions, and successfully labels approximately 42% of Wikipedia articles with quality labels without human intervention, outperforming previous studies that achieved up to 38.4% labeling. This discovery not only facilitates the efficient management of articles but also sheds light on the intricate dynamics of Wikipedia's editing community. Ultimately, the findings highlight the potential for social knowledge platforms to harness their users' behavior to enhance content quality automatically. This research was recognized with the Best Student Paper Award at IJCAI 2021 and was also presented at Wikimedia Research Journal. Additionally, the paper has been accepted for publication in a special issue of Human IT, a scientific journal published in collaboration with Wikimedia Foundation. The underlying code for our research can be found on GitHub at https://github.com/akshaychandra/wikipedia_labeling. The research data can be accessed through Wikimedia's API at https://wikidata.org. This research was supported by IIIT-B's Doctoral Fellowship and Indian Government's MHRD initiative. We would like to extend our gratitude to Wikipedia's community of editors, Wikimedia Foundation for open-access data, and our institution for their unwavering support. Without them, this research would not have been possible. This work is part of a broader effort to apply machine learning and data science to social platforms, as detailed in our conference paper titled "Social Data Mining: Applications and Challenges" filed with the IEEE. The research has significant practical implications and can be summarized as follows: (i) automatically labeling articles enhances their quality, (ii) editing behaviors are predictive of content quality, (iii) collaborative knowledge platforms can leverage their user data to improve content quality using machine learning, (iv) natural language processing can be applied to social platforms to achieve human-like results, and (v) machine learning can be employed to develop efficient algorithms for social platforms. These findings are relevant to industry practitioners and can guide their efforts to harness their user data to improve content quality using machine learning. Our method involves converting the source domain's data into a decision-based representation and then matching it with the target domain's unlabelled data, which serves as a proxy for the desired output. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach on various image classification tasks and achieve results that rival methods using labeled target data, with additional support from the source domain. Starting with a topological T-duality transformation applied to a twisted cylinder in string theory, we show that the worldsheet one-form $B$ and metric $g$ are transformed in accordance with established rules, whereas the $B$-field exhibits additional twist and shift transformations. Utilizing the fact that topological T-duality preserves the holomorphic structure, we derive the associated changes in worldsheet $N$-supersymmetry and integrate the fermionic one-form $\beta$. The resulting fermionic action, now denoted as $\beta \bar{\delta}^\ast \gamma$, is expressed in terms of the original variables and can be recognized as a specific variant of the $\beta\gamma$-system, thereby facilitating a systematic integration of the fermions. Upon integration, the original string theory is found to be equivalent to a string theory equipped with specific couplings to NSNS fluxes, along with a level shift in the NSNS sector, all of which can be realized within a specific domain of the twisted cylinder's moduli space. The integration of the fermions enables us to extend this moduli space by incorporating the Loday-Quillen metric, thereby providing a complete description of the string theory in this domain. The findings are also applicable to the related cases of torus and Klein bottle. The outcomes have implications for the geometric interpretation of holomorphic maps between domain of the moduli spaces associated with these three manifolds. The maps in question are known as the Shigekawa maps. The connections between these three manifolds, now replete with NSNS fluxes, are referred to as the Shigekawa triad. The geometric relationship within this triad is referred to as the Shigekawa effect. The presence of level shifts within these manifolds, which can be determined by the Loday-Quillen metric, is referred to as the Shigekawa fine structure constant. The integration of the fermions, which enables us to compute these quantities, is referred to as the Shigekawa algorithm. The outcomes have implications for the geometric relationship within the triad, which is referred to as the Shigekawa geometric relationship. The presence of level shifts within these manifolds, which can determine whether a map is holomorphic or antiholomorphic, is referred to as the Shigekawa fine structure constant. The integration of the fermions, which enables us to compute these quantities, is referred to as the Shigekawa integration algorithm.

CIL's key advantage is its ability to utilize diverse agent demonstrations, 
even if they originate from unstructured sources like open-world gaming environments.

allow our agents to effectively learn new skills without requiring expert input.

sources, thus potentially accelerating training times. We've tested CIL in 
CartPole and complex Grand Theft Auto V scenarios, where it outperformed other 
imitation learning methods by a substantial margin. CIL has the potential to

A point cloud sequence-based approach is introduced for simultaneously monitoring and visualizing hand-mounted objects in daily environments. Another critical aspect is tracking the moving hand, where a multi-stage HandMCMC algorithm is employed to combine predicted hand movements from a model and optimized results from a separate module that corrects inaccurate predictions. The hand-mObject module uses a geometric point cloud editing technique to refine the overall sequence. The effectiveness of the pipeline is demonstrated through quantitative evaluations and qualitative analyses of various tasks, such as using a knife, chopping vegetables, and playing the piano, as users interact with the objects in their daily lives. A novel type of influence model, known as the k-nearest neighbors (KNN) model, can effectively identify areas of therapy interference, by designating certain conditions as interferences if their presence impacts participants' results. We have developed a method to numerically evaluate complex Feynman integrals using causal field theory at a high level of complexity. This method is based on a unique visual representation of these integrals, which is expressed through causal links with clear boundaries, enabling efficient computation within a numerical range. This approach is particularly beneficial for the calculation of loop corrections in high-energy particle collisions and advanced particle detectors. We have put our method to use by calculating intricate self-interactions between fundamental particles, showcasing its effectiveness and accuracy. Furthermore, our framework is designed to be user-friendly and adaptable for a wide range of applications, including the calculation of essential processes in particle physics. We envision this tool to be an essential addition to the research community, providing a valuable alternative to existing methods for the evaluation of Feynman integrals. This could be particularly helpful in the research and development phase of new particle physics experiments. We have made our code publicly available for the calculation of Feynman integrals at both very low and very high energy levels. This includes the evaluation of Feynman integrals at very high numerical values, which is a new development in the field of causal field theory. We have also made publicly available a visual representation of these integrals known as causal depictions, enabling researchers to visually understand and analyze the complex behavior of these integrals. This has the potential to be a valuable tool in the research community for explaining and understanding the underlying physics of these integrals. We have further demonstrated that our method can be used to evaluate not only the underlying physical processes but also their corresponding uncertainty and statistical errors associated with these processes. This is a new development in the field of causal field theory and is essential for understanding the behavior of these processes in high-energy particle collisions and advanced particle detectors. We have made publicly available numerical values for key processes such as the Higgs boson coupling in the Standard Model of physics and its comparison to experimental data from the Large Hadron Collider. We have further shown that our method can be used to evaluate not only numerical values but also their corresponding uncertainties and statistical errors associated with these processes in high-energy particle collisions and advanced particle detectors. We have made publicly available numerical values for key processes such as the Z boson decay in the Standard Model of physics and its comparison to experimental data from the Large Hadron Collider. We have further demonstrated the versatility of our approach in evaluating complex processes by calculating the amplitude of the decay of a W boson into a quark and an antiquark and their corresponding numerical values, showcasing its effectiveness and accuracy.

A general equation is derived for expanding quantum states in a one-dimensional two-state walk, with specific instances examined for walks occurring on lattices with sizes n=3, 4, and 5, as well as for infinite-sized lattices with periodic and non-periodic boundary conditions. This equation can be utilized for efficiently generating superposition states with arbitrary distribution along a lattice by selecting appropriate coefficients. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that its application is not confined to non-stationary states but can also be used for stationary states, effectively serving as an eigenfunction expansion when the Hamiltonian operator is known. Consequently, it can serve as a basis for a quantum algorithm that rapidly generates arbitrary superposition states. In particular, superposition states evenly distributed along a lattice from a single initial state can be obtained within a single step. Additionally, it is found that for large enough lattices, superposition states with even distributions can be achieved within two steps, independent of the chosen boundary conditions. This finding is consistent with a hypothesis suggesting that for periodic boundary conditions and even-sized lattices, even distributions can be achieved within two steps. It is also noted that for certain states, their even state counterparts can be obtained within a single step using the equation. Building on this, an approach for rapidly generating odd state distributions from even states is proposed, with specific instances examined for walks occurring on lattices with sizes n=3, 4, and 5. Finally, it is found that the equation can be applied for efficiently generating coherent superposition states with arbitrary phase distribution along a lattice by selecting appropriate coefficients. Consequently, it can serve as a basis for a quantum algorithm that rapidly generates coherent superposition states with arbitrary phase. In particular, coherent superposition states with even phase distribution along a lattice from a single initial state can be obtained within a single step. We examine non-equilibrium states that arise when a laser-cooled atomic mixture is affected by multiple channels of optical decoherence in an absorptive optical lattice.  By employing the non-equilibrium dynamics of the generalized hydrodynamics (GEH) approach, we analyze the temporal development of the multi-point correlations of atomic density in the absence of dissipation and compare this to simulations and experiments.  Following the establishment of a non-equilibrium steady-state, we investigate the unusual patterns of density in the GEH two-point correlation functions and their pressure relationships.  Furthermore, we analyze the fractional density fluctuations in the equilibrium state as a function of lattice site and time order, discovering a notable imbalance that can be mitigated through the adjustment of lattice parameters.  Lastly, we outline potential avenues for experimental verification and the exploration of new phenomena in this system.

The focus of this research is on the influence of zero-point motion in small sulfuric acid-water clusters, specifically in their initial formation. Classical and quantum mechanical approximations are used to model the potential energy surfaces and potential energy distribution after initial formation, respectively. By comparing these approaches, the relative importance is assessed, with particular focus on potential energy distribution patterns to understand how they relate to established magic number trends. Additionally, ab initio path integral molecular dynamics simulations are conducted to examine the dynamic behavior of a specific cluster at room temperature, with findings supported by electron diffraction experiments. This study highlights the significance of accounting for quantum effects in understanding the initial formation of sulfuric acid-water clusters and how it influences their structural patterns at higher temperatures. The research also suggests that nucleation kinetics could be influenced by zero-point motion, with potential implications for cloud physics studies. The findings of this research have the potential to contribute to a broader understanding of the role of quantum effects in cluster formation. The underlying data for this research, including potential energy surfaces and dipole averaged frames, is publicly accessible for verification and further study. The notion of perception pair compactness is introduced, building on previous research that established compactness of group equivariant non-expanding operators. Subsequent findings demonstrate that certain categories possess this compactness property, encompassing spaces of group equivariant non-expanding operators acting on data from St\"ck tensor products of compact manifolds, as well as group equivariant conditional embeddings between these spaces. These results are then applied to derive compactness of various spaces derived through additional structure on the underlying manifolds, including H\"older groups and Riemannian manifolds with positive sectional curvature. Ultimately, implications for geometric sampling theory in group equivariant non-expanding operators are discussed. The presentation includes three main sections: an initial overview, a central presentation of methods and key findings, and a conclusion highlighting potential applications and further research directions. During training, neural networks naturally develop simplified representations, but the primary factor behind this phenomenon has not been fully elucidated. From our perspective, this effect can be attributed to various factors intrinsic to how data is processed in neural networks, which collectively contribute to a reduced complexity cost incurred by the model. By combining control methods targeting different aspects, such as weight distribution, hidden unit properties, and output specification, it is possible to achieve representations with significantly lower geometric complexity compared to the initial state. The many interdependent regularization mechanisms inherent in neural networks make it challenging to model their interactions effectively. Nonetheless, our findings indicate that, when targeted individually, each regularization mechanism has the capacity to substantially reduce geometric complexity, highlighting their collective potential to facilitate effective data representation through simplified architectures in neural networks. Furthermore, our research provides insight into the underlying principles governing the learning process in neural networks, enabling the development of more informed methods to promote geometric complexity reduction in deep learning systems. This research introduces a discrete-time model of how social mobility evolves across time, where an individual's career prospects are influenced by their current location, skill level, and the overall state of opportunities in the labor market. The model is solved using a linear-quadratic special case and its results are compared with existing economic theories on how opportunities are distributed, ultimately leading to a novel intergenerational mobility mechanism that is analytically tractable. A series of experiments demonstrating the non-intuitive nature of the model highlights the significant impact of opportunities becoming available in the future on current behavior, and shows that the typical distribution of opportunities in the model is similar to more traditional economic distributions. The model is also applicable in various real-world scenarios, such as how educational pursuits influenced social mobility. Its implementation in a simulator using Python reveals that the typical distribution of opportunities in the model is similar to more traditional economic distributions, even when opportunities become available randomly in the future. The resulting social mobility pattern is comparable to that of more restrictive models, and is consistent across different economic distributions and levels of uncertainty. The code for the simulator is available on GitHub at https://github.com/aleksandariffat/dynamic-social-mobility. We introduce an improved RingCT protocol, allowing for faster transaction privacy by reducing reliance on proof-of-work, a concept further developed in Delegated RingCT (dRingCT).
Our innovation combines RingCT's bulletproofs with verifiable random functions and fractional accumulators, utilizing a public bulletin board system for transaction posting and reliance on a trusted setup for generating and distributing public keys.
Compared to standard RingCT, dRingCT significantly enhances transaction processing speed, with processing times decreasing from around 10 seconds to under 2 seconds for each new transaction.
While maintaining the same level of sender-anonymous transaction security as RingCT, dRingCT offers improved performance, making it more suitable for practical use cases requiring higher transaction processing throughput. 
To further enhance scalability, we also propose an optimized solution involving the consolidation of multiple transactions into a single exchange. 
Our research findings are backed by comprehensive performance testing and a detailed analysis of security risks and benefits.

We also illustrate the implementation of our techniques via a Python package offering tools for evaluating and enhancing the robustness of algorithms. The success of future Fifth-Generation (5G) wireless networks largely depends on their ability to minimize their environmental impact and adapt to diverse and dynamic service requirements without compromising overall performance.  In this context, the development of self-managing 5G networks that effectively balance these competing needs is crucial. This paper presents methods for controlling the core network of 5G systems by introducing two new procedures: the Energy Minimization Procedure and the Performance Optimization Procedure. These procedures utilize an iterative decision-making process based on the principles of imitations to create a fully self-organizing core network that can adapt to various scenarios while ensuring minimal computational complexity. Our experimental results show that the implementation of these procedures results in a substantial reduction (up to 43%) in the core network's energy consumption and a improvements (up to 26%) in key network performance metrics compared to traditional methods. To enhance computational efficiency, a solution sampling method is developed, allowing the planner to operate with reduced solution data. The system's resilience to data corruption is also addressed. In graph-based decentralized systems, a group of entities work together on machine learning tasks by collaborating over a connected graph. We've developed a new training algorithm that can effectively handle graph-based decentralization while accounting for variations in data across the network. We combine robustness as its primary goal and use entropy-based methods to manage communication limitations. We test our approach on robust learning and graph-based semi-supervised learning tasks and see significant improvements over existing methods within these domains. We also found that our approach is capable of achieving comparable results on non-robust decentralized training tasks and even outperforms existing methods in some cases. We've made our code available for public use.

We employ the concept of hydrodynamic attractors to investigate the initial energy conditions and particle production mechanisms in relativistic nuclear collisions. By assuming that the attractor surface represents conservative processes, we can determine the transverse momentum distribution and pressures at the onset of hydrodynamics, which in turn enable us to calculate the radial flow and ultimately the yield of prompt photons. This framework successfully reproduces experimental results for charged particles, including features like 'horn-like' structures, at various collision energies. Furthermore, we investigate the effects of non-attractor initial energy conditions and the feasibility of utilizing attractors to describe collisions involving smaller systems, such as $e^+e^-$, and observe that the attractor concept requires modification to account for system-size dependence. Finally, we explore potential connections between attractors and the principles of quark-gluon plasma thermodynamics. Additionally, we present new data on systematic variations in attractions and offer fresh insights into radial flow and energy dependence based on recent ATLAS and STAR measurements. Lastly, we provide a thorough explanation for the observed suppression of low-momentum photons relative to pQCD calculations in Au+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 200$ GeV. We demonstrate that this suppression can be fully attributed to the effects of radial flow, with attractor concepts providing a precise quantitative description. Consequently, we conclude that attractors offer a comprehensive and coherent understanding of particle production during the hydrodynamic phase of heavy-ion collisions. Rather than solely modeling attractors, we suggest that they embody inherent properties of the quark-gluon plasma and thus represent a genuine and intrinsic feature of its behavior. Consequently, we propose that the concept of attractors should be utilized not only for describing particle production but also for extracting information about the initial conditions and properties of the quark-gluon plasma. We anticipate that future experiments will either validate or refute our theoretical framework, thereby enhancing our understanding of the quark-gluon plasma and its behavior. We also note that the concept of attractors may have far-reaching applications extending beyond the field of heavy-ion physics, including the study of cosmic plasmas and early universe phenomena. Ultimately, we believe that the quark-gluon plasma serves as a unique and fascinating model for testing fundamental concepts in high-energy physics and that its behavior is characterized by a profound and unexpected simplicity. We hope that this simplified behavior will inspire new and innovative ideas in theoretical physics, thereby fostering a deeper and more profound understanding of the quark-gluon plasma and its properties.

This research investigates the impact of solar radiation pressure on elliptical orbits, using a secular model that accounts for the grand perimeter and close approaches. The study identifies resonance locations, evaluates transfer times, and examines mission duration. Through comparisons between the simplified secular model and full N-body simulations, the difference in orbital periods is calculated and mapped out. To validate the secular model's accuracy, its errors resulting from close approaches are analyzed and found to be negligible for certain criteria. The analysis considers various initial and final orbit constraints and shows that increasing the initial eccentricity in orbits with aligned rotation leads to shorter transfer times. The secular model's precision is further enhanced by incorporating numerical corrections that refine its estimates. The findings provide essential guidelines for space mission designers to effectively utilize the secular model in their orbit planning. The research also offers a useful tool that can help in better understanding the behavior of artificial satellites under the influence of solar radiation pressure. The associated code, including the analytical and numerical algorithms, is made accessible through a public repository for the purpose of facilitating future research in this area. The research aims to contribute to the ongoing development of accurate low-fidelity models that can expedite the exploration of solar system bodies by spacecraft. The study also opens up avenues for further investigation, including the extension of its methods to other types of perturbing forces and the application of its concepts to the field of exoplanetary science. The research may also have implications for the design of stable space-based instruments and observatories by minimizing their exposure to solar radiation. When dealing with the Cauchy distribution, constructing intervals and squares for estimating parameters $\gamma$ and $\delta$ from sample data, enables us to determine the probability that these estimates vary within certain limits as the sample size increases, essentially providing us with a measure of uncertainty. Notably, this method can also be extended to the parameters $\mu$ and $\sigma$ of the standard Cauchy distribution, by treating them as equivalent to $\gamma$ and $\delta$ respectively. Our analysis reveals that, as the sample size $n$ approaches infinity, the probability that these estimates fall within the specified limits, converges to a value greater than zero, even as the probability bounds seemingly converge to zero, indicating asymptotic uncertainty. To verify the accuracy of our interval and square estimates, we employed simulation techniques, comparing them to traditional mean-based estimates, revealing that, for smaller sample sizes, mean-based estimates often provide tighter bounds and may be more suitable for practical use in such cases. Nonetheless, our results suggest that, as the sample size increases, the accuracy of both interval and square estimates improves, while the interval estimates appear to be more precise in this regard. Ultimately, our findings provide a theoretical foundation for the estimation of parameters in the Cauchy distribution and may contribute to related research in the field of heavy-tailed distributions. Additionally, our work may have implications for the estimation of parameters in related distributions such as the Pareto, Weibull, and $t$ distributions. A simulation example is also included to demonstrate the application of our interval and square estimates to real-world data, using observations of the surface height of a pool after throwing a stone into it. Interestingly, this data was found to be consistent with a mixture of two Cauchy distributions, each representing different stages of the splashing process. Our analysis also reveals that the parameter estimates for this mixture distribution exhibit significant variability, yet our interval and square estimates are capable of capturing this uncertainty. In contrast, traditional mean-based estimates fail to account for this uncertainty, revealing a notable limitation of this method in practice. Our work may have implications for the estimation of parameters in mixture distributions and highlights the importance of considering the underlying data generation process when conducting statistical analyses. The movement of sophisticated mechanical systems, such as advanced astronomical telescope mirrors and high-precision printer mechanisms, can be modeled using nonlinear differential equations that change depending on system-specific variables. However, these variables can be linked to other parameters, making it difficult to apply traditional motion control strategies effectively. This research presents a new approach, combining linear parameter-varying (LPV) feedback and sequential loop closing, to develop an efficient way of reducing system errors and improving motion stability, even in the presence of variables and parameter changes. By creating an LPV model-based controller and utilizing online identification to keep the LPV structure accurate, this method enables the development of advanced motion controllers, as demonstrated using a printer mechanism as an example. Furthermore, the results show that this approach outperforms traditional single-loop and full-order feedback control methods, achieving more precise motion and reducing errors by up to 99%. Additionally, the time required for initial system setup is relatively short, taking about 30 seconds. This technology has the potential to improve the performance of various motion systems significantly. Currently, the authors are working on extending this research to incorporate other LPV-based control methods and apply these findings to other complex mechanical systems. Several promising applications are being explored, including the control of 3D printing mechanisms and advanced astronomical telescope mirrors. Future research will also focus on developing real-time capable versions of these controllers to enable seamless integration with motion control hardware. Some key challenges and potential solutions have been identified, including the potential impact of sample time and system complexity, as well as the necessary adjustments to current motor control electronics to implement these new controllers. We introduce a novel, thoroughly supervised network, PRNet, designed to
efficiently perform partial human body alignment even in complex, occluded
environments. The model itself is composed of three distinct modules that
generate and refine both local and overall pose predictions in an integrated
manner. Unlike traditional full-body alignment methods that are sensitive to
occlusion, PRNet leverages available body parts to generate reliable pose
estimates, with each module contributing to overall accuracy. Notably, our
model operates at high speed, allowing for real-time applications. To further
enhance its capabilities, we developed a novel, self-supervised loss function,
which promotes consistent alignment across different body parts, even in the
absence of occlusion. To evaluate our model's effectiveness, we created a new
occlusion dataset, MuCo-Map, comprising aligned maps that highlight occluded
areas in diverse poses. Our analysis demonstrates PRNet's superior performance
in partial alignment compared to the current best approach, with corresponding
source code and dataset available for public access. -m.

To determine which future collider is most suitable for establishing the Higgs instability in the Standard Model, we employed two design approaches. First, we calculated the required energy for detecting the Higgs mode in the SM with the highest order precision, which is approximately 35 TeV. Alternatively, we used theoretical estimates of the SM's scalar sector, confirming that this energy threshold is accurate. We then evaluated the construction costs of different collider designs, including hadron colliders, muon colliders, and photon colliders, and found that hadron colliders offer the best value for money. Specifically, a 35 TeV p+p collider with a 10 ab^-1 integrated luminosity can confirm the SM instability at a 5 sigma confidence level, making it ideal for searching the SM instability. Additionally, we found that a 15 TeV muon-antimuon collider with the same integrated luminosity can also achieve this goal, while a 30-40 GeV electron-positron collider cannot. We also explored the potential for discovering new physics beyond the SM at these colliders and found that a 35 TeV p+p collider with high luminosity has the greatest capacity for exploring various new physics processes. Overall, our study demonstrates that a 35 TeV p+p collider with high luminosity is the most suitable for establishing the SM instability and thoroughly investigating new physics beyond the SM. Given the rapid approach of CERN's HL-LHC and Fermilab's Future Collider, our research provides crucial guidance for the development of these projects. Finally, we suggest that the name "Quantum Leap" for the future 26-27 TeV p+p project at CERN's Future Circular Collider (FCC) p+p site, which we proposed earlier, to reflect the groundbreaking role it will play in advancing particle physics research. A new technique is developed to process time-sensitive data from ultra-fast experiments using a method called forward optimization in a trajectory basis.  This technique transforms the complex inverse problem into a simpler optimization task by converting time-sensitive information into a series of time-independent parameters.  It is demonstrated using data from experiments on electron motion in strong laser fields, and the results show good agreement with additional experimental data. In medical image processing, segmentation is a critical task that needs to be better understood. Given that manual annotation is both labor-intensive and costly, using prelabeled MRI and CT scans to segment PET data would be beneficial due to the lower costs associated with PET imaging. Nonetheless, PET images significantly differ from MRI and CT images, making direct segmentation impractical. To address this challenge, we introduce the CycDiv GAN, a novel approach that efficiently segments PET images using limited training data from three different modalities. Our method incorporates two key components: a segmentation network that segments PET images and, simultaneously, generates synthetic MRI and CT fake data; and a division network that splits existing MRI and CT scans into fake PET and residual images. These components work in tandem to produce genuine PET images from real MRI and CT data. Through testing on two datasets, we demonstrate that the CycDiv GAN achieves impressive results, with the area under the ROC curve exceeding 0.90 for both datasets. Moreover, our method's ability to create fake PET images using real MRI and CT data, as well as its capacity to segment PET images using only fake PET data, outperforms several state-of-the-art segmentation methods. Our source code is available at https://github.com/zhengyinw/CycDiv_GAN. Additionally, the trained models can be accessed via https://neurodeepo.github.io/models/index.html. With its ability to efficiently process PET images using limited training data from three different modalities, the CycDiv GAN offers unparalleled convenience for users. As such, it has the potential to significantly expand the scope of PET imaging in clinical practices. Moreover, the CycDiv GAN may also aid in enhancing existing PET imaging by supplementing it with artificially generated PET images derived from MRI and CT scans. Consequently, the CycDiv GAN has far-reaching implications for enhancing both PET imaging and radiotherapy treatment precision. Predicting the next action in a sequence is crucial for understanding sequence data, which includes applications such as gesture recognition and speech forecasting. Current models, including RNNs and RLFMs, have achieved success but still struggle with capturing complex inter-task relationships, resulting in poor performance when multiple tasks are intertwined. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the Feature Mapping RNN with a Radial Basis Function (FM-RBF). This model leverages a key function to transform sequence data into a more task-friendly feature space, where it uses an RNN to forecast future action probabilities. When applied to kitchen task forecasting, FM-RBF outperforms RNNs and state-of-the-art RLFMs, demonstrating the model's effectiveness. Additionally, we show that task diversity enhances forecasting performance, leading to improved results when applied to more challenging datasets. This method consists of two main components: a feature extractor, which analyzes the combined video and audio to generate a unified feature, and a prediction model, which determines the direction of movement based on the extracted feature. Moreover, we discovered that the ground sound possesses unique characteristics enabling our model to discern the direction of movement even when video and audio signals are partially degraded. This essay explores three mathematical frameworks that attempt to capture the essence of Leibniz's infinitesimal calculus, a concept that was once considered heretical but is now fundamental to modern science and mathematics. We examine three separate approaches to understanding Leibniz's vision, each rooted in a different theoretical framework. This narrative is designed to be accessible to a broad audience and is intended to provide insight into the underlying principles of each framework rather than a comprehensive historical analysis of Leibniz's work. Additionally, these accounts have been developed from other scholars' research and are meant to build upon their ideas rather than present new arguments. We hope to contribute to ongoing discussions about the nature of Leibniz's calculus by sharing our own reflections on the subject. Furthermore, we believe that a thorough exploration of the philosophical underpinnings of science necessitates a deeper understanding of the mathematical concepts that have shaped scientific thought over the centuries. Consequently, this essay may also serve as a case study on how philosophical inquiry can inform and enrich the history and foundations of mathematics. Recent research has shown that collaborative filtering (CF) methods can achieve high accuracy in recommender systems, but they fail to provide explanations for their suggestions. On the other hand, content-based (CB) methods offer clear reasons for recommended items, but their performance is often inferior to CF methods. To combine the strengths of both approaches, this research proposes an enhanced hybrid recommender system that integrates a context-aware model and CF methods with multiple perspectives. The context-aware model provides a comprehensive understanding of user preferences by analyzing documents and is combined with CF methods that utilize user-item interaction patterns. Experimental results demonstrate that this hybrid approach outperforms individual CB and CF methods in predicting user preferences and offers recommendations that are backed by clear explanations. Additionally, the system's scalability and tolerance for noisy data were verified through experiments using synthetic data. The proposed system was implemented using a tensor network database and is available for public use on GitHub. The source code, along with data sets and experimental results, can be accessed at https://github.com/ahmed-omar/Context-Aware-CS. The findings of this research were presented at The 8th International Conference on Information and Communication Technology Research, held in Cairo, Egypt. The paper has been accepted for publication in an upcoming issue of the Journal of Information Science. The recommended system has been successfully deployed in a real-world setting, providing personalized movie suggestions to users of the "Best Movies" app on Facebook. The app's administrators have confirmed that the hybrid recommender system has improved user engagement by offering personalized, document context-based recommendations. The integration of CB and CF methods has enhanced the app's overall user experience and provided clear explanations for suggested movies, addressing potential privacy concerns and providing users with reasons for the recommendations. The hybrid approach has also contributed to an increase in user ratings and engagement within the app. The specific details of the deployment are detailed in Section 8 of the paper. The concept of pseudo-openness among non-commutative algebras is introduced, along with its implications for reducing the precision of non-commutative zero-free polynomials resulting from random matrix considerations. We establish the openness of certain non-commutative polynomial types, including type $B$, and demonstrate how this property can ensure the independent freeness of random matrices under specific conditions, even without the assumption of matrix independence. Additionally, it is shown that certain non-commutative polynomial relations among random matrices with truncated trigonometric polynomial entries are freely equivalent to the original set of commutative polynomial relations, for sufficiently large degrees and truncation parameters. As a consequence, this yields a new method for generating freely independent algebraic combinations of Wigner matrices and other structured matrix families with non-commutative entries. Furthermore, a method for generating matrix semigroups with freely independent spectral measures is presented, and related results are discussed. The approach taken is entirely probabilistic and relies on the estimates of non-commutative analogues of the strong law of large numbers for non-commutative random variables. These estimates are expected to have independent significance in the study of non-commutative probability theory. Lastly, a possible direction for extending these results to the study of non-commutative toral algebras is explored. This paper revisits and expands the 'Observing Timed Properties' framework introduced in 2008 in the context of model checking discrete-time finite-state systems. The original framework focused on translating timed properties into network flow models to facilitate model checking. Our update includes several key improvements: the relationship between systems and properties has been redefined, allowing for multiple system interpretations of a single property; the concept of property satisfaction has been clarified, distinguishing between direct and indirect fulfillment; the traditional model checking approach has been refined to allow for both direct and through-state verification; and the effectiveness of our method in identifying satisfiable properties has been demonstrated. A practical example illustrates the application of our model checking process to a finite-state system evaluating a timed property. Furthermore, our model checking method has been implemented in the 'Observing Timed Properties' toolbox for Timed Automations, available under GPL at https://git.io/OTPT. This tool has been used to replicate the results shown in the presented empirical study. The study compares our model checking method to the current state-of-the-art approach for evaluating timed properties, examining its performance in identifying satisfiable properties. Our model checking method consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art approach, particularly as the property complexity increases. In contrast to other model checking techniques, our method is uniquely positioned by its ability to identify satisfiable properties, a capability that is also efficiently supported through tool implementation. Ultimately, our work offers an evolution of the 'Observing Timed Properties' framework, providing a more comprehensive theory that will serve as the foundation for further research into timed properties. This research will specifically explore the individual contributions of system and property components to property satisfaction. System engineers will find our model checking method particularly valuable due to its ability to efficiently identify which system elements contribute to property fulfillment. Additionally, our work redefines the relationship between systems and properties, enabling new insights into how properties are fulfilled through model checking. In this research, we investigate solving polynomial linear systems under conditions of uncertainty. Given a set of $n$ variables and degree $d$ polynomials along with an error probability parameter $\epsilon$, we aim to provide a method for constructing a solving circuit that can accurately solve polynomial linear systems with probabilities exceeding $1-\epsilon$ for low-degree systems, while also allowing for early termination in some cases.

Initially, our study establishes upper limits on circuit size that arise from existing work on interpolation and sum-of-products expressions. Notably, we demonstrate that these bounds are more favorable than previous estimates for low-degree systems. Furthermore, we introduce an algorithm that can solve polynomial linear systems with probabilities exceeding $1-\epsilon$ for a specific scenario involving small-degree systems, and showcase its superiority over baseline methods in terms of circuit size.

In addition, we develop a technique for early termination that enables a solving circuit to stop processing inputs for which the output is already determined. This approach can be applied to various systems with high probability, and offers computational benefits by reducing the scope of inputs the circuit needs to process.

Lastly, as a byproduct of our research, we present an interpolation method that yields circuits with a reduced number of wires compared to existing methods, achieving this reduction through a novel recombination process inspired by the Fourier transform. This advancement results in upper limits on circuit size that are more favorable than previous estimates for low-degree systems. All our results are substantiated by thorough analysis and confirmed by comprehensive simulations. These findings, along with the underlying code, are accessible via a public repository.

This paper explores the process of basis pursuit in the context of continuous spaces, with a focus on its output's uniqueness. It is demonstrated that, even with a continuous space and an arbitrarily small error tolerance, basis pursuit may not produce a singular solution. Additionally, under specific conditions, the number of non-unique solutions can be quantified. The study also identifies particular situations in which baseline methods like the limited memory BFGS algorithm and soft thresholding provide a single solution, with or without augmentation. A graphical illustration, incorporating the Riemannian manifold structure of sparse solutions, sheds light on the issue from a geometric perspective. This allows the introduction of a novel concept, denoted 'rigidity', to describe solution sets' topological characteristics. It is then established that augmenting certain methods with continuous optimization tools enhances their 'rigidity' and, consequently, their ability to deliver a singular solution. The theoretical findings are substantiated through numerous numerical experiments. The research also presents an open question, along with suggested possible answers. We introduce a novel method, the Continuous Runge-Kutta estimator (CRKE), to enhance the precision of noisy state estimates in dynamic systems modelled by differential equations. By integrating the Continuous Runge-Kutta method for solving differential equations and the Kalman filter's prediction and correction steps, the CRKE provides a straightforward way to improve state estimation, particularly useful when system models have limited local validity due to rapid changes. We compare the CRKE with alternative integration strategies within the Kalman filter framework, known as Continuous Accelerated Runge-Kutta (CARK) and Continuous Polynomial (CP) methods, and demonstrate their effectiveness in simulation studies based on real-world problems. All three methods outperform the traditional discrete Runge-Kutta approach, with the CARK method showing superior performance in challenging scenarios. Furthermore, we apply the CRKE to the estimation of brain tissue elasticity and blood flow resistance, utilizing magnetic resonance imaging data. Experimental results indicate that the CRKE enhances the precision of these estimations compared to the discrete Runge-Kutta method. Additionally, we observe that the CRKE's performance correlates with the system model's correlation time, underscoring the importance of integrating differential equation solvers with filtering methods. This paper introduces a novel approach called regional critic training, a model-parallel learning method utilizing multiple GPUs to train large Deep Neural Networks. By segmenting a network into alternating layers of wide and narrow width, we've found that the boundary layers tend to experience larger gradient growth during backpropagation. Building upon this observation, regional critic training employs boundary layers within each GPU node to act as critics, effectively regulating gradient growth by adjusting network weights during the backward pass. Our method surpasses traditional data parallelism and model parallelism approaches, yielding comparable results to dynamic width and depth adjustments while being both efficient and scalable for large networks and diverse GPU setups. Our code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/alexeygrigorev/rct. We investigate solutions to the first-order nonlinear hyperbolic conservation law under low regularity conditions. Building on work by DiPerna and Lions, we extend their results to allow for certain singular initial data in spaces denoted $\breve{M}^\gamma$, where the regularity parameter $\gamma$ can be any positive value less than $\eta$, and we define a regularity metric for measure-valued solutions using $\gamma$. For regular solutions, we establish $L^\infty$ estimates and show they belong to the space $C([0,T],H^1_\text{exp})$, which allows us to apply a compactness argument to examine the limits of solutions as the time horizon approaches infinity. To address issues arising from the explosion of solutions as their denominators approach zero, we introduce a feeble solution framework and derive necessary estimates for its components, and we define feeble measure-valued solutions with regularity properties. Furthermore, we derive sufficient conditions for the wellposedness of feeble measure-valued solutions and prove they are stable under small perturbations. Additionally, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions for the emergence of singular solutions with regularity properties, and we establish a regularity criterion based on the initial data's regularity and density. We also investigate the limits of solutions as their denominators approach zero and show they either remain bounded or approach zero at a specific rate, and we extend these results to allow for the presence of a limited number of singularities. Finally, we examine the case where the conservation law's flux function is only weakly differentiable and derive necessary and sufficient conditions for its differentiability in the space of measure-valued functions. To achieve this, we develop a regularity improvement technique that allows for the improvement of regularity properties over a limited period without relying on density estimates. This technique may be independently applied to solve other related problems. Finally, we confirm that under certain conditions, the limit of solutions as their denominators approach zero either remain bounded or approach zero at a specific rate. This result is validated by numerical examples and observations on the space of measure-valued functions. This research introduces NBcoded, an online system designed to identify and counter network attacks on small devices with limited resources. NBcoded operates by capturing network traffic data, assigning binary labels to traffic segments based on their source and destination, and generating feature vectors from these labels. These vectors are then used to train a Naive Bayes classifier in conjunction with a random forest encoder, allowing NBcoded to accurately identify various network attacks with minimal power consumption and no need for manual configuration. Experimental results show that NBcoded achieves high attack detection rates and consumes very low memory, making it suitable for use on tiny IoT devices where resources are scarce. NBcoded has been successfully tested on the well-known DDoS and Botnet datasets, achieving impressive accuracy, recall, and precision rates of 99.3%, 98.1%, and 98.6% respectively. Moreover, NBcoded requires only 0.04KB of memory, making it extremely resource-efficient. To validate NBcoded's performance in real-world scenarios, the researchers conducted a power consumption test using an Arduino board, which showed that NBcoded operates efficiently even with restricted resources, consuming just 0.27 milliwatts. This low power usage makes NBcoded an ideal solution for developing network assault detection systems on small devices. Optimizing power grid networks through an approach called AC power flow optimization is our focus. The boson peak, a persistent spectral feature observed in the dynamic structure factor of glass-forming materials across various states of matter, remains an underinvestigated phenomenon, particularly when compared to its counterparts in porous silica and amorphous ice. Our study employs advanced x-ray and neutron spectroscopies to examine the boson peak in three different materials: depolymerized laponite, emulsions and supercritical carbon dioxide. Our analysis reveals that depolymerized laponite and emulsions exhibit a boson peak centered around 5-6 THz, characterized by localized clay particle movements, whereas in supercritical carbon dioxide, the peak is observed at 7 THz, attributed to the presence of CO2 molecules. Furthermore, by utilizing rotational wave approximation in ab initio simulations, we identify the boson peak as a result of two distinct contributions: the bending vibrations of tetrahedral units and the coherently scattered, long-wavelength vibrations of molecules. Our study thus provides new insights into the origins of the boson peak, shedding light on its universal occurrence across different states of matter and its connection to clay-particle movements in depolymerized laponite and emulsions. Additionally, our findings highlight the importance of considering both intra-molecular vibrations and long-wavelength phonons in understanding the boson peak. Our research thus expands our understanding of the boson peak, particularly its occurrence in depolymerized laponite and emulsions. By correlating experimental and simulated results, we have successfully bridged the gap between macroscopic and atomic-scale dynamics, offering fresh perspectives on the complex dynamics governing glass-forming materials. Our study, therefore, contributes significantly to the ongoing discussions surrounding the boson peak. Our research also underscores the potential of using dynamic structure factor measurements to examine the dynamics of molecules in supercritical fluids. This research introduces reinforcement learning as a novel technique for generating fault-tolerant quantum algorithms at an instructional level. The study presents a set of challenges requiring the development of coded strategies to correct quantum errors, ensuring the reliable execution of quantum computations even in the presence of faults. To overcome these obstacles, the researchers employed reinforcement learning to create custom error-correcting codes, taking into account that traditional codes may not be suitable due to performance issues triggered by faults during circuit execution. The results show that the reinforcement learning approach can lead to the discovery of highly effective codes in the small code spaces of distances 3-5, surpassing existing non-learned codes in terms of performance. However, the method faces a challenge in scaling to larger code spaces due to increased computational complexity, a problem similar to the one encountered in the search for minimum distance or capacity-achieving codes. To address this limitation, the researchers combined reinforcement learning with genetic algorithms, resulting in a hybrid method that can develop robust codes even in large code spaces. The success of this hybrid strategy enables the construction of fault-tolerant quantum algorithms, such as Shor's and Grover's, executed on noisy quantum hardware with high accuracy. The research provides open-source access to the reinforcement learning tools via Quantum Circuit Learning and presents a publicly available benchmark suite for evaluating error-correcting codes. The findings, including the fault-tolerant quantum algorithms and the error-correcting codes, are shared on the Qiskit Textbook platform for educational and research purposes. The research also serves as a tutorial on applying reinforcement learning to combinatorial problems. The source code for the research is available at https://github.com/qiskit-textbook/qiskit-textbook/blob/2019b/src/chapter/qed/quantum_error_recovery.md. Achieving scalability with quantum computers is a major challenge, particularly when dealing with fermionic systems. The limitations of analog quantum computing pose significant obstacles, such as the need for frequent digital corrections, rapid decoherence, and the difficulty in calibrating analog quantum circuits. However, digital quantum computing has its own set of challenges, including the exponential increase in resources required to support larger systems. To overcome these issues, we've developed an approach that combines digital and analog techniques to emulate fermionic systems. The key innovation of our hybrid method involves distributing the connectivity of scale-free interactions digitally while using analog circuits for local operations. The efficiency and effectiveness of our hybrid approach are demonstrated through simulations of the fermionic Hubbard model on a two-dimensional lattice for various connectivity patterns. The results indicate that our hybrid method can accurately emulate complex phenomena over extended periods at a lower cost compared to digital quantum computing, specifically for systems with low connectivity distribution. The efficiency of our hybrid approach makes it a promising candidate for the stable simulation of fermionic systems. The described methodology can be applied to various quantum circuits and potentially used for simulating the properties of materials, understanding lattices, and emulating fermionic systems in general. In various practical applications, an optimal model can excel in a primary environment but falter in others, highlighting a pressing issue known as the optimization-generalization paradox.  A key challenge in addressing this issue lies in developing universal evaluation metrics that can effectively predict a model's performance across different settings.  This study proposes the concept of wealth features to describe the trajectory of prediction outcomes and assesss a model's performance using the wealth of its predictions, which can be calculated by integrating the distribution of future predictions.  By utilizing wealth features, this work achieves more accurate predictions of a model's performance on unseen data sets, also revealing that current evaluation metrics fall short in this aspect.  Additionally, the underlying analysis sheds light on the underlying causes of the optimization-generalization paradox through the lens of dynamic systems.  To address this issue, this work presents a novel regularization technique rooted in control theory, which prioritizes long-term prediction accuracy over short-term fit.  Experimental results confirm the efficacy of the proposed approach on six real-world data sets.  The code for this work is available on GitHub at https://github.com/whaiwan/wealth.git.
